speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We have the Naval College. What, then, is this vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is for schools of navigation such as have been carried on for many years. These schools are for the instruction of men who wish to pursue navigation, to get certificates as mates and captains. The schools give instruction in the use of nautical instruments, and so on. These schools are established at ports throughout the country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is nothing new in this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No; such schools have
been carried on for many years.
Does the Government pay anything to the Technical College in Nova Scotia for carrying on classes in navigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Government is arranging to establish a school of navigation at Halifax in connection with the Technical College.

Will a sum be
voted this year for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It will be paid for out of this vote. Correspondence is going on now between the authorities of the college and the department on the subject.

I would strongly
commend the idea of the Government assisting the Technical College at Halifax to

establish a school of navigation. I think that this work of education could be carried on by the college more effectively than by any other means. At present, it is the practice of the Government to make small allowances to persons at various ports who will conduct navigation schools for limited periods during each year for the instruction of persons desiring to go up for examination. I think experience has shown that this is not very satisfactory. In a comparatively small province, such as Nova Scotia, suitable educational facilities in navigation at Halifax, I should think, would meet all the requirements of the province generally. A well-equipped school at Halifax would probably attract a greater attendance than schools distributed throughout the province. I trust arrangements will be definitely concluded between the department and the college.

I have drawn the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, on more than one occasion, to the necessity of a branch school at Canso. Five or six years ago a school was started at that point in the winter season, and the attendance was quite large, running as high as forty, I believe. But recently the grant to this school has been withdrawn. I am not accusing my hon. friend of doing that for any improper purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That grant was withdrawn before I became minister.

That i3 not the point I am making. The proposition to establish a school of navigation at Halifax in connection with the Technical College should embrace also branches at places along the coast such as Canso. A sailor cannot afford to go to Halifax and epend two or three months in getting his education, and we ought to bring education to him. Along the coast we have a large number of young men, hundreds of them, engaged in the fishing industry. These men are partly idle during February and March, and this would be a suitable time for them to get instruction. I cannot help thinking that the proper system would be not only to have a central school at Halifax, but to have branches along the coast in various places where sailors could have an opportunity of getting this instruction; they could go up for examination at Halifax. We have two or three of these schools already, but they have never been supported by the Government to any considerable extent. The

small pittance that the teacher gets does not make it worth his while bothering with it at all, and the institution hardly deserves the name of a school. A small amount given to some retired sea captain who chooses to gather around him a few sailors, is about ail that is done. If we are going to give education of this kind, we ought to follow out some definite system that would be worthy of the people of Canada. I am not specially accusing the present Administration; we have never had an Administration in this country that has taken an interest in this matter. We have been pretending' to be doing something for the education of our seamen ever since Confederation, and all we have done is to appoint gentlemen in various places along the coast to instruct, in the great art of navigation, such sailors as choose to come to them. I would like to see the department doing something bigger than that. If the technical school is the right place-and I think it is

let the head school be placed there, but let us have, not only Nova Scotia but in the other Maritime provinces, branches at various points along the coast where the young men can get an education to fit them to pass the examinations and obtain licenses. It would not involve a very great expenditure, and I submit it would be a good departure for my hon. friend the minister to make.

I concur very heartily in the suggestions made by the hon. member for Guysborough, and would suggest that the minister apply them to the Baie des Chaleurs, around which there are five constituencies, Northumberland, Gloucester, Restigouche, Bonaventure, and Gaspe. In these constituencies no facilities are afforded to the young people to enable them to receive an education of this kind. In Gaspe and Bonaventure we are hundreds of miles from Quebec, St. John and Halifax. There are no facilities of any kind so far as instruction in agriculture is concerned, and perhaps the Department of Marine and Fisheries might set a good example by making a start in navigation instruction. We have a population consisting largely of seafaring men, and some educational facilities should be afforded them. During the long winter months in the Gaspe peninsula, aside from the lumbering operations, there is very little for the young people to do, and I am sorry to say that at present hundreds of them wander into the state of New York, the Ottawa River district, and elsewhere, to

engage in lumbering. Those who do not go to the Ottawa River district go to the United States, and, in many cases, are lost to Canada. I submit that an opportunity is here afforded for the taking of steps by which these young persons may be kept at home and their time properly occupied during the winter months. A start might be made in one of the constituencies- say at Bonaventure River, in the constituency of Bonaventure, where we have a population of 2,500-by giving a course lasting, say a month. The same might apply to Grand River, in the county of Gaspe, to Bathurst and to other points on the south shore of Baie des Chaleurs. These points on the south shore are within easy access of St. John and Halifax, but such is not the case with points on the north shore. In winter the county of Gaspe is sometimes deprived of railway communication, and only very difficult communication is afforded even with the county of Bonaventure. If the minister came forward with a new departure in this respect it should meet with support from both sides of the House. I concur in what the hon. member for Guysborough has said, and I hope the minister will apply his good intentions to the Baie des Chaleurs, and especially the north shore.

So far as I am concerned, I have no objection whatever to the most generous financial assistance on the part of the department so far as the starting of navigation schools is concerned. Of course, as there would be a limit to the number of schools, there would be a limit to the amount required, but I doubt very much if the idea which my hon. friend the hon. member for Bonaventure has in mind will meet the situation, or that the establishment of schools by constituencies is a feasible or practical idea. The difficulty in establishing successful navigation schools lies in obtaining pupils. The hon. member for Guysborough and the hon. member for Bonaventure will agree that if you cannot get pupils to attend the school, the same is a failure.

The thing has never been tried in the peninsula. Because it is so remote and difficult of access, the conditions in the peninsula of Gaspe are quite different from those of the northern constituencies of Nova Scotia.

I doubt if the inference my hon. friend desires can be d^awn from the conditions existing there. Schools have been established at many points in
Nova Scotia, and difficulty has been found in securing pupils to attend them. The hon. member for Guysborough says that they have no difficulty in that regard in his constituency-this I am glad to hear-and that the attendance is very good. But that was not the experience in other places in Nova Scotia. However, I think it would be wise indeed to assist navigation schools in almost any district in any province where there is a demand for such a school, but I think the idea of a strong central school is advantageous. I know that in Nova Scotia more masters and mates obtained certificates when there was a very good marine school in Halifax conducted by a private individual, whether aided by the Government or not I do not know. This was some twenty or twenty-five years ago. The advantage. of association of students or applicants for certificates was very beneficial; it caused the students to take a greater interest in their work, and this advantage is absent in a small place where there is an attendance of only half a dozen or a dozen. I think, too, that there would be a very considerable advantage in having a strong navigation school in some central part of each province, with such a provision for schools in the other outside districts as has been suggested by the hon. member for Guysborough.
How many men qualified last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This year there are schools at Vancouver, Collingwood, Quebec city, North Sydney, Halifax, Yarmouth, and St! John. Of these seven schools three are in Nova Scotia, one in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, at North Sydney, One at Yarmouth, and the other at Halifax, in connection with the technical college. The appliances and instruments required have been purchased and are now at Halifax, and as soon as a suitable building is obtained the school will start. I am in sympathy with the idea advanced by the hon. member for Bonaventure that perhaps we would reach those who want an education in this respect better by a number of small schools than by a central school, because if you have these schools in cities, as a rule the young men who may want to take up navigation as a profession are not men of large means, and it would be easier for them to attend a school in a smaller center than in a large city. They could not afford to go to the-large cities.
On the contrary, they are usually well off; that is, they are young seamen with ambition enough to want to secure certificates.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
But these are usually
young men who have only been before the mast and most of them are men of rather limited means. Last year we had no school at either Halifax or St. John, although those are the two largest shipping ports in the Maritime provinces. There was no school at Halifax owing to the illness and subsequent death of Captain Lugar. At page 29 of the report of the deputy minister the following information about the schools will be found:
The following tabulated statement shows where the schools were held, the total number of lectures delivered and the total attendance at each:
	Total Lectures.	Total Attendance.
		
Collingwood. Ont. .	32	361
Halifax, N.S		5	
Quebec, P.Q	43	753North Sydney. N.S.	30	242Vancouver, B.C. . .	15	178Yarmouth, N.S. . .	30	161155	1,695
There was one lecture and thirty-eight in total attendance less than during the previous year which is accounted for by the illness of Captain Lugar, of Halifax, which disorganized that school. A noticeable increase in attendance occurred in the eastern schools, while the total daily attendance at Vancouver fell from 707 last year to 161 in 1912.
The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) asked the number who obtained certificates. The numbers are as follows: in the eastern division, 70 masters and 38 mates; in the inland division, 85 masters and 37 mates; and in the western division, 43 masters and 48 mates.
How many passed as masters and, mates at Yarmouth?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall ask the deputy
minister to obtain that information for the hon. gentleman and send it to him.

I was surprised at the large number who passed at Yarmouth, and I think it would be a great pity if it was intended to have a large central school at Halifax and to do away with the smaller schools.
Mr.' HAZEN:	We have no intention of
doing away with the schools at Yarmouth and North Sydney .
What proportion of the grant is to be paid to each of the navigation schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We did not use the full amount of our grant last year. I think the sums run from about $300 to $600.
I understand that Colling-wood is the only school in Ontario. Is it necessary for a candidate to go to Colling-wood to pass his examinations or secure a certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Collingwood is the only school in Ontario, hut no change has been made in reference to passing examinations or securing certificates. This may be done at a number of places as heretofore.

I would endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) in reference to having schools in each of the constituencies of the north shore of New Brunswick and the Bay de Chaleurs. On the north shore there are many young men who wish to pass the examinations but cannot afford to go to St. John, Halifax or Charlottetown. Many times young men come out oi superior schools with an aptitude for navigation but they are not able to attend these navigation schools. Only two years ago two young men coming from the school of Mr. Boudreau, from which many good seamen have come, wished to pass their examinations but they were not able to afford to go to one of the cities referred to for that purpose and they went into some other occupation. Until the minister can establish more schools he should have his examiners visit many more localities in order that young men desiring to pass their examinations may do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) that our policy now is to send the examiners to definite points when any young men wish to be examined. I know what my hon. friend refers to: there was no examination of masters and mates last year in the province of New Brunswick, but we sent an examiner from Charlottetown to Chatham.
The young men had to go to Charlottetown to pass the examinations.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, I was just explaining to fhy hon. friend that our policy now is to send the examiner to the point that would be most convenient, and that last year in

order to enable a number of young men on the Miramichi to take their examination, we sent the examiner of masters and mates to Chatham where the examination was conducted. We intend to follow that policy in future. I agree with my hon. friend that it would be very unfair if young men from places like Bathurst and Dalhousie had to go to Prince Edward Island or to St. John to pass the examinations.

I wish to emphasize
what has been so well said by my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and by my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr.. Turgeon). I formerly represented one of the counties on the Baie des Chaleurs. The idea of my hon. friend to decentralize as much as possible the schools of navigation, is an excellent one. I remember, when I was member for the county of Gaspe, I used to receive every year a number of requests for passes over the Intercolonial railway or on steamship companies running down to Quebec and some points on the coast of Gaspe, from sailors. These young men have to earn their daily bread and are not generally well off and when they have to travel quite a distance in order to try their examinations, they quit. And what is the result? From letters I have received this year from different priests in the county of Gaspe, I learn that this winter the parishes have been completely depleted of the young men. Their trail can be followed to the United States navy, or to the shanties in the state of Michigan, or the Upper Ottawa district, and many young men who go as sailors in the United States or to the lumbering camps, do not return. I have noticed that there is quite a colony of my old Gaspe electors in the city of Ottawa. I daresay there are almost 500 or 600 people here from the counties of Gaspe and Bonaventure. They have been lured by the city and they will not return to the deep sea fisheries.
Are they all in the public service?

The same thing might be said with regard to the city of Montreal and possibly the city of Quebec. In Montreal, in Gaspe street, Hochelga ward, there are at least from 1,000 to 1,200 natives of Gaspe, and we can trace the preponderance of Gaspe electors in that ward to the fact that no facilities were provided at home to enable them to learn seafaring. They have been lured by the cities and have stayed in the cities. In the 48
counties of Gaspe, Gloucester and Bonaventure, there is a large population of French-Canadians, Acadians and Jersey fishermen. The old fishing establishments of Robin and Colas, and Le Boutkillier and Cie, have for over a century sent their ships to Italy and Spain, where the Canadian fish trade used to flourish. Some thirty years ago the trade began to go in another direction, and they sent their fish to the West Indies and to South America. At that time we had on the Labrador coast, and in Gloucester county and in Gaspe, deep-sea captains who had travelled all over the world, but to-day it is only by accident we meet one. The reason for this is that the young men who are horn sailors have not been encouraged, and no facilities have been provided for them to learn their trade. I would urge upon my hon. friend the necessity for decentralizing the schools of navigation, so that our young men in the Maritime districts should be given a chance to become deep-sea captains as their forefathers were.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will be very happy to give instructions next year for one of the examiners to proceed along the coast of Gaspe or Bonaventure, as may be most convenient, for the purpose of conducting examinations.

I would suggest that
my hon. friend confer with that very excellent officer of his, Commander Wakeham, who knows the coast by heart and practically every family there. I am sure he would give him excellent advice as to the places where the examinations should be held. I think myself that they could very well be held at Pointe aux Esquimaux, on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, at Gasp6 basin, Mount Louis, Perce and Grand river on the south shore. I am sure that the department would find that the young men on the coast, having such facilities to pass their examinations, would become what they were born to be, excellent sailors.

Do I understand that the minister is merely going to send down an examiner? I suppose some course of instruction would have to be given. There are hundreds of young men down there who, when they arrive at a certain age, do not know what calling to enter. They are born seamen, they have breathed the salt air from the day of their birth, and'if some course of instruction is not provided for them they may go to the United States and



disappear from the Baie des Chaleurs district altogether. My idea is that some preliminary school of instruction should be established and a course of lectures extending over two or three months in the winter time, given. I think in that way you would have excellent subjects for the examination next season. I do not suppose it is the intention of the minister to send an examiner down there, and no one to instruct the young men.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A great many of those who come up for examination have never attended the schools provided by the Government. In many parts of Canada there are private schools, kept by gentlemen who have been sailors or navigators and, where these private schools are in existence, it is not the policy of the Government to interfere with them by establishing a school. But from the remarks of my hon. friend the conditions along the Gaspe coast must be different. My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has convinced me that it would be only proper and right that we should during next season establish some school along that coast for young men who desire to study navigation. I will see that that is done.
Mr. MARCH.: I can assure the minister that the attendance at Bonaventure will be satisfactory from the start.
Ocean and River Service-Registration of shipping. $3,000.

In connection with the item relating to the registry of ships, it would be interesting to know how many ships have been withdrawn from Canadian registry during the year and what tonnage has been added. It is commonly supposed that the laws relating to shipping are a little too stringent in Canada, and the result is that a good many ships owned by Canadians are taken off the Canadian registry and registered in other colonies like Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: And Barbados.

Barbados. It has been
a common occurrence in my province for some years past. One of the chief reasons for this is that coasting captains are restricted in the latitude in which they may sail. There i? no reason for this restriction, which did not exist until some years ago, and which was made more istringent than was necessary. At the present time a coasting captain has a right to clear from a Canadian port and to sail to any point north of Central America. There are a number of points farther south of that

latitude to which coasting captains would often like to sail. My hon. friend can take the newspapers in the city of St. John, or city of Halifax, any day, and I will venture to say that he will find clearances for ports on the coast of South America, ports like Rio and Bahia, and other points on the River Plate. A coasting captain cannot legally clear for these ports under the present law. He must be a deep sea captain to do that. The coasting captain goes to the custom house and, when he says that he is clearing for a port south of t'he latitude allowed by law, the customs house officer refuses him a clearance. In certain ports in the province of Nova Scotia I have known it to happen that some old man who had obtained a license a good many years ago, would be sent to the customs house to get the clearance, and when the vessel got down to a point some distance from the port of sailing the old man would be sent home and a young man who had a coasting license only would get on board and take the vessel to a point beyond the latitude stated in the law and no question would be asked. That is a device that used to be resorted to-I do not know if it is still resorted to-in order to get rid of this difficulty. There is no reason why a coasting captain should not be allowed to go down the coast of South America. Let him go to South America and let him go around the Horn if he wants to. I would like the minister to facilitate a Bill which I have introduced in order to give coasting captains their right to go farther south than they can go at the present time. I do not know anything about the circumstances or conditions on the Pacific coast, but I looked up the law and I found that a coasting captain on the Pacific coast can only go -as far as the harbour -of Portland. That? is not very far from Canadian territory. I see no reason why that limit should not be extended.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think a coasting certificate in British Columbia enables a man now to go as far as San Francisco.
I did not know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think there was some amendment a few years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter to which my
hon. friend refers is one of great interest to shipping men in the Maritime provinces and also to those on the Pacific coast who are engaged in the shipping trade. On the Pacific coast I understand that captains can go as far south as San Francisco, and I think their desire is that a coasting certificate shall enable them to go even farther south. There is no doubt that what my hon. friend says is correct, that a great many coasting vessels are being registered in Newfoundland, Barbados and at other points where no certificated captain is needed at all. In addition to that there are vessels owned by St. John companies which are registered in the state of Maine, notwithstanding the fact that they are managed by St. John people. I have had rsoiesentations made to me by the owners of coasting vessels both in Halifax and St. John, and I have had conferences with some of these gentlemen in St. John. One gentleman came to see me just before New Year's. It was in connection with the new Canada Shipping Act which I propose to introduce to Parliament this year. The introduction of that Bill will afford an opportunity for a full discussion of this entire question. The owners of coasting vessels want to have the right to receive a coasting certificate which will enable them to proceed right down to South America all along the coast, and they argue, and argue with a good deal of force, that a man who is able to take a vessel from a Maritime province port down along the coast of North America as far as Cape Hatteras is quite capable of taking a vessel down the coast of South America. They say that it is difficult to get certificated captains and almost impossible to get certificated mates. They ask, first, that the certificate shall entitle a captain to take his vessel farther along the coast than he is now permitted to do, and that the certificate, in so far as the mate is concerned shall be abolished altogether. Some also have told me that there are cases where they get men who have a certificate, but whose age precludes 48}
them from being of any use, to simply take the vessel from port and the voyage is continued under that certificate. There is a diversity of opinion about the matter, but I think it is a question well worthy of consideration, and I intend in the next week, or the week after that, to introduce a Bill which will be a consolidation and revision of the Canada Shipping Act. I doubt very much if an Act of this importance, and containing so many sections, ean be passed through the House this year, but I shall suggest, on the second reading of the Bill, that it be referred to the Marine and Fisheries Committee of the House, before which there will be every opportunity of discussing all these questions which are so important to the shipping interests of Canada. I am only offering my personal opinion now, but I think it would be in the interests of Canadian shipping if some modifications were made, and, while if) would be in the interests of Canadian shipping, I do not think it would in any way imperil the lives of those who go to sea or tjie property which is entrusted to the men who handle these vessels.
Mr. MARCH,: I might inform the hon. minister that circulars have been received by members of the House lately protesting against the coastwise business being done by Norwegian vessels. Is there any new feature of the question, or does the same arrangement continue to subsist as that which has been in existence for some time by which Norwegian vessels are allowed to engage in the coasting business?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is nothing new in
that matter; it is exactly the same arrangement as that which has existed for many years.

To be continued until
1913 under a treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, I do not think there
is any treaty about it.
I thought it was in view of a treaty between Norway and England which allowed Norwegian vessels to come into British colonies.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so.
The people of Nova Scotia protest very strongly against this.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The vessels bring coal from Nova Scotia up the St. Lawrence. That privilege was given some years ago; I believe there was very little objection to it,

and it was extended for a period of one year when it expired a couple of months ago.
Is not there a general protest by the shipping interests of the Maritime provinces against that privilege ? I see that the gentleman who signed the circular is very severe.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not seen the circular.

I will send my hon. friend a copy of it.
Ocean and River Service-Removal of obstructions in navigable waters, $20,000.
How is this $20,000 to be expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In 1912-13 we spent only $1,533 of the vote.
There were no obstructions last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. In 1913-14, we spent $1,179. The officers of the department are of the opinion that it is impossible to estimate with any accuracy the amount that will be required. If hon. gentlemen will look at page 5 of the departmental report of this year, they will see that the following obstructions were removed during the year:
Florida, sunk in Montreal harbour. Scow Newel Hubbard, sunk at Hocket Beach. An old barge sunk, entrance of Chateauguay river, P.Q. A derelict in Vancouver harbour, B.C., S.S. Joliet, sunk in St. Clair, Ont.; and logs from Victoria harbour, B.C.
There have been years when the whole amount is required. In other years only a small portion is required.
This item is only for the removal of wrecks and obstructions in navigable waters, and not for the removal of obstructions in rivers ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This item is not for the removal of snags and other obstructions from rivers. That work is attended to by the Department of Public Works. In some of the rivers where lumbering operations are carried on, and there is a good deal of navigation, the practice of the Department of Public Works is to give a charter to some tug-boat owner to go to those waters and to remove obstructions. Sometimes a log will be found standing straight up in the water, and a steamer running into it might suffer great injury. This item is for the removal of derelicts in navigable waters.
Does not the department make a claim when the obstruction is taken away ?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We do. The owner of the vessel is responsible for removing it, and we at once notify him. If he does not remove it, we do so and proceed against the vessel owner and make him pay.
What is the necessity of the vote if the money is collected from the owner of the vessel ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The vote is necessary because we need some fund from which we can pay for the -work before we collect from the owners of the vessels.
5	p.m. There are always cases in which the vessel owners cannot be collected from.
In the cases mentioned by my hon. friend, has the Government been recouped ? .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the case of the Joliet which was sunk in St. Clair, we were recouped. The owner refused to pay; we proceeded against him and forced him to pay.
In the case of the barge sunk in the Chateauguay river, were you recouped ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, it was an old barge, and we apparently could not find anybody whom we could compel to pay.

I have been able to find the circular to which I referred, and I shall read some extracts for the benefit of the minister:
Are Norwegians still to monopolize Canadian coastwise trade? Or is it to be Canada for Canadians in our coastwise trade, which means the transport of our products from one Canadian port to another Canadian port? Build up Canadian coastwise shipping. Trade follows the flag.
A few years ago Nova Scotia's tonnage was 558,000. In 1910 it had declined to about 160,000 tons, mostly fishing schooners. The province of Nova Scotia at one time owned more shipping tonnage per head of population than any other country in the world. Canada has been reduced from the fourth shipping maritime power in the world to eleventh place.
Then there is a letter which appeared in the New York Tribune under date of September 28, 1913, from Alexander T. Baillie, a resident of Port Hastings, Cape Breton, Canada. Then there are Orders in Council and memoranda from the Department of Customs regarding the coast trade of Canada. One of these, dated December 8, 1911, reads as follows:

Steamships of not less than two thousand tons gross tonnage each, of the following countries, namely:	Norway Sweden, Austro-
Hungary and Japan shall be admitted to the coasting trade of Canada in the carrying of goods and passengers coastwise between any port in the province of Nova Scotia and any port in the province of Quebec, and vice versa, on the same terms and conditions as are applicable to Canadian vessels, until the 31st day of December, 1915.
John McDougald,
Commissioner.
It concludes by a pathetic appeal headed:
Heroic Nova Scotia seamen who risked their lives to rescue those on board the ill-fated Cobequid.
Then other criticisms follow. The conclusions are these:
A few years ago Nova Scotia tonnage was 658,000 tons; If her coastwise trade and seamen had been protected as some other important industries in our province, such as coal, she would have to day over one million tons of shipping instead of about 160,000 tons mostly fishing schooners.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Of course my hon. friend will understand that that matter does not fall within the jurisdiction of the Department of Marine and Fisheries; it is a matter of the Department of Customs. I understand that Mr. Baillie has been protesting for some fifteen years against it, but the governments during that time, after considering the matter, have seen fit to extend it. Without this extension it would be very difficult for coal men to get their coal to Montreal. They could not get it there on terms that would enable them to sell it at a profit to the consumer if they could not take advantage of these Norwegian bottoms.
Is it the policy of this Government to stop the granting of these licenses at the end of the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot tell my hon; friend what the policy will be. There is no decision on the matter.

From 1907 or 1908 to 1911, it was just as much the policy of the party which is now in power to prevent the matter to which the bon. member from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has been referring as it was to give this country adequate protection, purity in elections, the Highways Bill and other things. I think the minister should give us some reason for not carrying out this programme. In some constituencies in Nova Scotia, particularly a county like Lunenburg, the electors there were promised by Conservative candidates that if they came into power, Norwegian vessels would not be permitted to engage
in Nova Scotia trade. In fact, pretty nearly every Conservative candidate in the election of 1908 was unequivocally pledged to prevent the continuance of this. Does the minister ever receive communications from his political friends in Nova Scotia asking that Norwegian vessels be prevented from engaging in this coasting trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This matter falls within
the control, not of my department but of the Department of Customs. I have never received any such lttters as the hon. gentleman refers to; but such letters, if written would, in the ordinary course, be addressed to the Minister of Customs.
Ocean and River Service-Winter mail service, $11,000.
Will the minister please explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This vote is given every
year to provide for the ice-boat service between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse, when the regular steamer service is cut off. In some years this whole vote is used and in others very little of it. In the season of 1912-13, the amount spent was $7,129.30, and for the present season up to January 1, only $91.23. Of course, the great expenditure may come in February and March.

I will ask my hon.
friend (Mr. Hazen) to do this year what he was kind enough to do last year-and that is, when the season is favourable, to allow one of the Government steamers to go from Prince Edward Island or Pictou to the Magdalen Islands. As the hon. minister knows the Magdalen Islanders are deprived of all communication for several months in the year. The last letter I received was from the Rev. Mr. Turbide, of House Harbour. He says: ' I am writing you, because fortunately, a steamer has come this morning, and from appearances navigation will be possible during six or eight weeks more. Some years ago the officers of the Marine Department found difficulty in inducing the cap-tajns to take the risk of this trip. But the experience of the last two years has proven that it is quite possible in an ordinary season for a steamer to cross to the Magdalen Islands.' The same remark applies to Seven Islands. The Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) knows that winter navigation between Quebec, or the mouth of the Saguenay river, and Seven Islands is quite possible. For several years the department has sent the Montcalm once during the winter months, and the people of that distant shore have had the privilege of receiving the mails. I would like to know

what is the intention of the minister this year with regard to that? Will he continue this service and familiarize the people of this country, and other countries with the idea that winter navigation is quite possible below Quebec? There are no insuperable obstacles to winter navigation between Cape Tormentine on the mainland and Souris, P.E.I. It has been demonstrated also that navigation is possible between Quebec, St. Catherines Bay, and Seven Islands. My hon. friend knows what a boon it is for those isolated people to receive mail during the long winter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Stanley has made one trip to Magdalen Islands this year, and we hope she will make other trips. The Montcalm returned last week from Seven Islands and is now engaged in ice breaking on the St. Lawrence. Mr. Forneret, superintendent of the ice-breaking service, said it was necessary to continue this work until next week, when we shall send the vessel to Murray bay. The hon. gentleman will see that we are doing the best we can to maintain communication below Quebec.	.

Will the Champlain
be soon ready for service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
She has been undergoing
repairs, and I am informed that she is ready. They are building a new wharf to afford her safe wharfage accommodation.

I understand that the
landing at Murray bay is quite difficult. But the Postmaster General will tell my hon. friend that there are other wharfs on that shore, viz.-Cap a l'Aigle, St. Irenee, Les Eboulements, Bale St. Paul. I am not sufficiently versed in navigation to .say whether a boat could easily land at those places, but an effort should be made, because the distance the people of the county of Charlevoix have to travel in order to reach the terminus of the Quebec railway is long, and mails from the city of Quebec are not delivered within a week. I would urge the hon. gentleman to do his best to afford the people of Charlevoix better facilities of communication.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Champlain is that,
being an ice-breaker, she is of deep-draught and would have trouble in reaching some of the wharfs to which the hon. gentleman refers.
In the summer the same boat will touch two of these wharfs-Cap a 1'Aigle and St. Irenee.
Will the steamers for the Magdalen Islands start from Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They generally start from North Sydney.
The Stanley made the last trip?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes; she is now at North Sydney.
I have had communications from the Magdalen Islands about this matter. Can the minister tell when the next trip will be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No decision has been
reached about that. The Stanley at this moment is engaged in ice breaking.

When a trip by the
Stanley to the Magdalen Islands is contemplated, I presume notice is given to merchants?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, that is done by the agent at Quebec.

In a Quebec newspaper
yesterday I observed that owing to the ice, the Montcalm has returned from an ineffectual attempt to enter Ellis bay, Anticosti, and that she intends to return there next Tuesday. Conditions at Ellis bay are very much affected by the wind; it might be filled with ice one day and be free the next. I hope the attempt to enter the bay will be kept up.
Ocean and river service-Cattle inspection, $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This item is incorrectly worded; it should read 'inspection of livestock shipments.' This vote is placed at the disposal of the department for the purpose of paying inspectors whose duty it is to see that the cattle and horses shipped from Canadian ports are properly provided for on the vessels. A few years ago quite a large amount was needed for this purpose, but the shipments of cattle from Canada are not as formerly. There are two inspectors at Montreal, Mr. H. Delorme and Mr. J. O'Grady, one getting $1,200 and the other $1,000 a year. There was an inspector at St. John, but the shipment of cattle from that port has practically come to a standstill, and as there is no necessity for the continuation of the office, it has been abolished. The few small shipments which do go out are looked after by the agent of the Marine Department.
Is there no hope that the cattle embargo will ever be abolished?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I really do not know.

I have no doubt that the system of inspection of livestock at Canadian ports is excellent, but when our cattle reach the other side of the water, they are prevented from going farther than Liverpool or other ports of entry, although we are an .exceedingly loyal people, and we have a superlatively loyal Government; at least the Government is self-assertive in that respect. Lasf year the Government gave evidence of its great loyalty by asking this Parliament to make a gift of $35,000,000 to the mother country, while in various other departments of the Government the greatest facilities are offered to our friends in Great Britain. I remember, when I was Postmaster General, I gave the British newspapers special facilities and special rates in order to foster a splendid British feeling in this country. Some years ago it was rumoured that pleuro-pneumonia had taken hold of our Canadian cattle, which as we know was nothing more or less than a libel. Sir Charles Tupper, writing I think about ten years ago, said that early in the eighties he took up that matter with the British authorities and proved beyond the shadow of a doubt that the assertion that Canadian cattle were subject to this disease was nothing more than a libel upon Canadian livestock. The reason or pretext given for the continuation of the embargo is the desire to afford a measure of protection to the north of Ireland grazing interests. As I have said, we have given to the mother country many evidences of our loyalty and goodwill. Is it not time that the Government should insist upon the removal of this embargo? What steps have this Government taken to redeem the excellent reputation enjoyed by Canadian cattle in former years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend will have to ask the Minister of Agriculture.

My hon. friend was in Europe two years ago, and he delivered loyal speeches before many clubs, including the Colonial Institute. He was the honoured guest of many associations, and he spoke of the good feeling existing between the two countries. I stand for the mother country, but I like to stand for my native land. As a good Canadian, my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and
Fisheries delivered many eloquent speeches when he was in England; he even lectured that loyal Welsh lawyer, the Rt. Hon. David Lloyd George.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is news to me.

Did not my hon. friend make a speech in England in which he said that the statesmen of Great Britain ought to do more for the navy, and not spend all the money of the people on so-called social reforms?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I made no such speech.

At all events my hon. friend gave advice to the Government of Great Britain as to their internal policy. Has he not been able to find time and words to ask the British Government to remove that embargo, and to give our Canadian cattle the standing they had a few years ago?
Did I understand the minister to say that he is not spending very much now on the inspection of shipments of cattle to Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, there is really very little spent.
As a matter of fact, are there any cattle going to Britain at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Last year the shipments were:	from Montreal, 178 sheep, 6,469
cattle and 175 horses.

That was in 1912-13. Of
course there was a very important event in 1914 which has altered the business altogether. In 1912, in the whole year, we sent- about 7,800 head of cattle to Great Britain; but in the month of November last, I read somewhere the other day, not one split hoof of cattle went to Great Britain, in the month of November. But 75,000 head, including calves, very unpatriotic cattle, went south.
Under which flag?

It might be drawn to
the attention of the Imperial authority that we are better treated in the United States than we are in Great Britain in regard to this matter. I understand that our cattle are shipped from various points and are admitted to the United (States without any question, whereas shipments to Great Britain have to be slaughtered as soon as they arrive. I think my hon. friend, who is familiar with these matters, ought to press the fact on the attention of the Iml

perial authorities that the people of Canada, in regard to this matter, are treated better by the United States thaij by the home 'authorities.
Mr. MICHAEL	CLARK:	On the
question of the embargo, I cannot quite endorse what ipy hon. friend from Guysborough and my hon. friend from Rouville* say in regard to that being originally a protective measure. I think the regulation was enacted in perfectly good faith by the old country Government. They believed there was disease amongst Canadian cattle, and it should be remembered that the herds kept in Great Britain by great agriculturists, from the occupant of the Throne downwards, are very expensive cattle and very valuable. I might admit that in Great Britain, as elsewhere, anything that has a protective tendency is much more easy to get on than it is to get off, and, with the very strong connection there has been between the Irish party and the Liberal party, which has been in power for a number of recent years, of course the weight of Irish opinion may have influenced the Government. I quite admit that, but I think that, in the early history of the embargo, it is scarcely right for my hon. friend to prefer a charge or even to hint that a charge of bad faith against the British authorities might be laid. I think the embargo was put on in good faith as a preventive of disease amongst the very valuable herds that are kept over there. But with the small number of cattle going now to Great Britain I cannot think that the embargo in Great Britain is a subject of very practical importance. The removal of the embargo elsewhere, which is after all the worst of all embargoes, the embargo of a protective tariff, has produced results which make the disease embargo fade into absolute insignificance.

My hon. friend misunderstood my remarks. I did not intend to cast any reflection on the good faith of the Imperial authorities, but I merely drew attention to the fact that we are better treated in the Unied States. It appears that when we want anything big done in this country we have to go to the United States for it. Nobody expects our own Government to do anything of importance in that line. We .know that the greatest thing done for Canada in 1913 was done at Washington. I want to emphasize the fact that we are very well treated across the line, and it would be worth while to im-

press on the Imperial authorities that they should give us the same treatment in Great Britain.

There is no doubt that the trade in live cattle between Canada and the United States is a very-important trade, and we do not want to have anything done or left undone that might endanger it. If this embargo on our cattle going to Great Britain is continued on the plea that our cattle are diseased, is there not a possibility and even a probability that the interests in the United States that are opposed to our trade in cattle with that country may bring that up and may use it as an argument against the importation of cattle from this country? It appears to me that this is well worth consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I fancy that the United
States knew of the embargo long before they admitted our cattle free to that country.

This is not a contentious matter; it is important looking to our export trade that if our cattle are not diseased everything should be done to remove the embargo between this country and Great Britain.
Mr. LEMlEUX:	In the matter to which
I referred a moment ago, I do not wish to quote the whole speech I delivered, but to refresh my hon. friend's memory. I said last year:
I was surprised to read the other day a speech reported to have been delivered in England by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries before the Imperial Maritime League. He said ' A mere gift of money will have no useful effect at all. The giving of money for the navy by the Dominion of Canada will merely have the effect of saving the pocket of the Liberal Government for other schemes of so-called social reform which, being interpreted, means further sops to the United Kingdom electorate and will be of no advantage whatever to the navy.' ,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
From what does the hon. gentleman quote?
Mr. LEMlEUX: I forget now. I got the speech from the papers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is the first time 1
have heard it. I never made such a speech as that. I do not think that any sane man going from Canada in a representative capacity would give utterances to such thoughts couched in such language. 1 would like to know the source of the report because it does not convey any idea of vhat I said on any occasion.
I am very glad to hear my hon. friend say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I saw something in a
Montreal paper which I corrected.

Who are the inspectors
in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. H. Delorme and Mr. O'Grady.

Does this inspection of cattle apply only to cattle for export across the sea? I would fear that there might he some conflict of authority with the Agricultural Department if there is an inspection for disease.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is not an inspection
for disease. It is an old vote to provide for the inspection of the accommodation provided for cattle on steamers, to see that they are put in proper pens and that proper provision is made for their treatment during ocean shipment. It applies only to cattle for shipment across the Atlantic.

I am glad that no obstacles
are put in the way of the trade in cattle between Nova Scotia and the United States, because our farmers are reaping quite a harvest now and we are looking forward to quite a large trade in cattle and other articles.
Wrecking plant, $45,000.
I would like to ask whether the Government still has the Davie establishment at Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Davie threw up the
contract a year and a half or two years ago. He was not able to make it pay. For several years there had been very few wrecks on the St. Lawrence and he made no money. He submitted his figures to the department and gave his reasons for giving up the contract.

Is there a wrecking
plant at Gaspe basin?
Where is this plant located?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The plant of the Quebec Salvage Company at Quebec, in the St. Lawrence. The Quebec Salvage Company is to maintain the steamer Lord Strath-cona and such other plant as may he required to the satisfaction of the department, from the first of May to the first of December, of each year while the agreement lasts. This boat does certain comber work within fixed zones and being equipped with wireless it can get quickly to the scene of a wreck.
Does all this grant go to that company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: What amount of money does the Dominion Coal Company receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: $10 and $25 goes to the Quebec Salvage Company under the conditions I have described.
Is the subsidy to the Dominion Coal Company subject to any conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. ,
And the British Columbia Salvage Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Does the minister propose to have a plant at Port Nelson?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No request has been made as yet.

Ocean and River Service-Unforeseen expenses, $5,000
What is this?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These are odds and ends which sometimes occur in the department. If my hon. friend would look at the Auditor General's Report, page N-44, he would see what items come under that head. The expenses for 1912-13 was S663.85.
Is that money used in connection with investigations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There might be investigations, not covered by other votes, which it would be used for.
Did Mr. Duchemin get any of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so.
There would not be enough there to pay Duchemin.

I have a file here brought down by the Department of Marine and Fisheries which contains an account, J. A. Gillies, for the Department of Marine and Fisheries, to W. Forgeson, dated 6th, 1912, It reads:
To railway expenses to Pictou, $1.95 ; steamboat, $1; to Mulgrave stage, $1, $3.95; May 8, 1912, to return from Pictou to Port Royal, railway expenses, stage and boat, $5.25 ; hotel and travelling expenses, $3.75; loss of time 3 days at $3, $9; telegrams to J. A. Gillies, &e., $1.45; telegrams to Marine Department, 50 cents', total $23.90.
(Sgd) Wm, Forgeson.
This struck me as rather an unusual account, inasmuch as it stands in the name of J. A. Gillies for the Department of Marine and Fisheries indebted to Wm. Forgeson, Port Royal. I would like to get some information as to why this account is here in the form in which it happens to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What page is that on?

Page 77 of a return to an order of the House dated April 7, 1913, showing a copy of all accounts, vouchers and charges incurred by and relating to the lobster hatchery at Arichat during the season of 1912, with the names of the officers and crews of the patrol boat Davies and the wages paid to each.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That. applies to the Fisheries branch, and I may say to my hon. friend that when we reach that branch I will have the information here for him. I never heard of it before.

I would like to ask if the minister has treated any other officials in

the way he beheaded Mr. Trefry, who occupied the position of shipping master at Yarmouth. The minister dismissed one of the best officials who ever occupied that position, and he was in such a hurry to dismiss him that he appointed a gentleman -I have nothing against him whatever- who was an American citizen. The minister was so eager to appoint Trefry's successor that the port of Yarmouth was without a shipping master until the new appointee could get his papers making him a British subject. Mr. Trefry had been dismissed, and we had to do without a shipping master until the new man could get his papers. I only wish to state these facts to the Committee to show the way in which the Marine Department have acted in connection with dismissals.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will give the House the facts in connection with Mr. Trefry:
In April, 1895, the shipping master at the above port was Mr. J. R. Rogers, who was dismissed in October, 1896, by Order in Council, owing to charges of political .partisanship. Captain John A. Tilley was then appointed shipping master in the room of Mr. Rogers. On the 11th November, 1896, an Order in Council issued dismissing jCaptain John A. Tilley and appointing Norman L. Trefry. On the 11th March, 1912, a letter was received at the department signed by Knowles E. Crosby, and several others, preferring charges of political . partisanship against Mr. Trefry. It was stated that Trefry had used every effort to defeat the Conservative candidate and to elect Mr. B. B. Law, the Liberal candidate. An affidavit was received from Dr. A. M. Perrin of Yarmouth, testifying that in the election of 1908 he solicited votes and drove a team to carry voters to the polls; that he attended a political meeting held by the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier at Digby, N.S., absenting himself from his office and duties; that he assisted to bring Mr. Law forward as the Liberal candidate at a caucus of the Liberals in September, 1911, at which time at the grand entrance of the S.S. Prince George of the D.A.R. SS. Company, he grasped the hand of Captain McKinnon bf the Prince George and stopping him on the stairway exclaimed :	* Ha, ha, we had a hard task to
induce Mr. Law to offer himself for a candidate, but he has at last consented after a deal of ' petitioning; ' that he took part in a political meeting held in the opera house at Yarmouth; when he was on the platform with Mr. Law.' In view of the representations in Dr. Perrin's affidavit, an Order in Council issued under date of the 10th April, 1912, dismissing Norman L. Trefry and appointing Captain Samuel Messenger, shipping master in his stead. .
What about his successor, an American citizen?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
His successor is now a
British subject.

It is only natural
to find another case of this kind. The people this Government appoint to office are American citizens. When they wanted somebody to investigate the so-called Transcontinental railway expenditure they were not satisfied to take a British subject, but they appointed Mr. Gutelius. He was not a British subject when he was appointed, and they proceeded to naturalize him in order that he might be a fit and proper person to investigate this matter. So, when we come to Yarmouth, if they cannot find in that county a good Canadian or British subject to be shipping master, and if they have to appoint an American citizen, it is a pretty curious state of affairs.

In reply to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I beg to say that Mr. Trefry absolutely declares that the whole statement is a falsehood. As far as I am personally concerned, I am prepared to state that Mr. Trefry never sat on a platform at any meeting that I held in the -county of Yarmouth in 1911. Further than that, Mr. Trefry did not attend the meeting held by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in Dighy. He was not out of the town at that time, but he was in Yarmouth attending to his business. Knowing Mr. Trefry as I do, I am prepared to state that his dismissal was one of the most inhuman of all the inhuman things that this Government has done. Mr. Trefry was a first-class official. He never attended any political meeting; he never was on a platform at any meeting held by me, he never attended a meeting at Digby, and I am surprised that, under the circumstances, he being a British subject, he was not considered entitled to have an investigation. "My opinion is that the minister was afraid to have an investigation because he knew that he would not be able to prove the charges against Mr. Trefry. I cannot understand for the life of me why this gentleman should not have been given the investigation to which he was entitled. The other day I asked the minister if he knew that there was a patronage committee in Yarmouth. He assured me that he did not know of any such thing. Let me tell him that Knowles E. Crosby is a member of that patronage ocmmittee, and why should Mr. Crosby's statement be taken when the minister did not know that he was a member of the patronage committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I informed my hon. friend that this statement was supported by the affidavit of Captain Perrin of Yarmouth.
Mr. Trefry tells me that the statement that he acted in a partisan manner is absolutely untrue. I only bring this matter up in order to put Mr. Trefry right before the House and the public.

The circumstances surrounding the dismissal of Mr. Trefry appear to call for the censure of this committee, but I think I can bring to the attention of the minister even a more indefensible case and one that calls for even more severe censure than that which we have just heard. At the opening of the session of Parliament in 1912, I put this question to the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries:
Has the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, received the evidence taken by H. P. Duchemin, commissioner at river Bourgeois, in the month of October last, on the charge of political partisanship alleged against Marin Bourque, keeper of the lighthouse of river Bourgeois, who was dismissed in the month of April last?
2.	Has any report been received from Mr. Duchemin bearing on the investigation?
3.	Is it the intention of the minister to reinstate Mr. Bourque as keeper of the lighthouse?
This question remained on the Order Paper from the beginning of the session until some time towards the 15th of January. This man Bourque was dismissed in the spring of 1912 without any investigation upon the ex parte statement of the Conservative candidate in the county that he was a partisan. The charge of partisanship made against Bourque was so outrageous that I felt that an investigation would show that it was without any foundation whatever, and that he should he reinstated in his office. An investigation was granted by the minister, and the commissioner went to River Bourgeois in the month of September. I was present when Mr. Duchemin called as the first witness Mr. William Levesconte, a leading Conservative there, and after he had been questioned by Mr. Duchemin no evidence was disclosed against Mr. Bourque. Mr. Duchemin was so insistent that Mr. Levesconte should ransack his memory to find some act of partisanship against Mr. Bourque, and he persisted to such an extent in the question as to whether he knew if this man had been guilty of partisanship, that the witness replied: 'How in blankety-blank do I know whether he had or not?-'blankety-blank' in this case indicating a place which is ' usually regarded as being the very antipodes of the abode of the blest. Knowing that evidence had been taken in an effort to prove a charge of

partisanship against Bourque, I put this question to the minister in the early part of the session of 1912. The question was allowed to remain on the Order Paper week -after week. His Honour the Speaker called it time after time, but the minister always asked that th-e question be allowed to stand. Some weeks after that Mr. Du-chemin sent a second report of the investigation which he had held into the same charges against this man Bourque. The first investigation disclosed no evidence against Mr. Bourque, and here is the answer given by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to my question:
1. The investigation referred to was arranged by Mr. Duchemin to be held on the 27th September, 1912. On that date no evidence was taken. A further inquiry was held on the 12th December, 1912.
If the minister was informed no evidence was taken on the 27th day of September, he was falsely informed. If he meant to say that no evidence to prove the charge of partisanship against Bourque was taken, then the statement is absolutely true. As a matter of fact, the evidence which was given by	the	witness	who	was summoned by Mr. Duchemin to give testimony against Bourque discloses no proof of partisanship against him. While the question remained unanswered upon the Order Paper, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries lest this man Bourque should escape the dismissal which had been ordered to take pl-ace	in	respect	to -him, ordereda second investigation	to be	held. Mr. Duchemin	the	second	time	co-mes to
Kiver Bourgeois to hold an inquiry; and as to the circumstances under which that inquiry was held, I will read a statutory declaration of Bourque's wife. Bourque was an invalid; his health was not very good at the time he was dismissed, and the effect of his dismissal and the prospect of being deprived of the $100 a year, which he was receiving by virtue of his being a lightkeeper, so diminished his ability to support his family that it resulted in aggravating his illness, and when Mr. Duchemin arrived the second time to hold an investigation, Bourque was upon a sick bed and was unable to attend the inquiry. His wife took to Mr. Duchemin the summons which her husband had received, and in this declaration I have a report of the circumstances which I shall read to the House after the committee resumes.

At six o'clock the House resumed, and then took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: House in Committee on Bill No. 17, respecting the Ottawa Northern and Western Railway Company.-Mr. Friop.

subsubtopic: OTTAWA NORTHERN AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Might we have some explanation of this Bill, either from the mover or from the Chairman of the Railway Committee?

subsubtopic: OTTAWA NORTHERN AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The Bill passed
exactly as it was sent to the committee. It is a renewal, and there was a renewal last year. The three standard clauses that we were so careful about were inserted last year. No objection was raised to the Bill as drawn.

subsubtopic: OTTAWA NORTHERN AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
What ground does the
charter cover, and what is the term of the extension?

subsubtopic: OTTAWA NORTHERN AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: This Bill is to amend chapter 84 of the Statutes of 1899 and chapter 72 of the Statutes of 1900. I have not these Acts before me, and cannot give exactly the geography of this line. It is to be commenced within two years and completed within five. That is the usual time.

subsubtopic: OTTAWA NORTHERN AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: There was no objection to it in the committee?

subsubtopic: OTTAWA NORTHERN AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
No.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: House in Committee on Bill, No. 11, respecting the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company.-Mr. Stevens.

subtopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The hon. member in
whose name this Bill stands will perhaps give us some information.

subtopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The amendments to
clause 1 of this Bill do not change the effect of it in any way, but merely improve-as we thought-the language. And there is a'repetition of the words: 'which is authorized to construct,' which we struck out. We added a third section to enact our present standard clause as to the water-
