speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: House in Committee on Bill No. 12, respecting the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company.-Mr. Douglas.
What is the purport of this Bill ?

To authorize the building of branch lines in southern Alberta,
where they are urgently needed. The matter was gone into very carefully by the committee and it is satisfactory. But the promoters have objection to an amendment put in by the committee, and if nothing is done in connection with that amendment I would ask that the Bill be allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: What was the amendment ?
It was in connection with the time when the work should be started and completed, and provided that it should be started within a year and completed within three years.

The majority of the committee thought that this was a case in which the company should be hurried up, and it changed the proposed time of commencing' from two years to one, and of completion from five years to three. The vote stood 22 to 10 in favour of the amendment. These matters, of course, are within the discretion of this committee, and I am not suggesting that it cannot reverse the decision of the Railway Committee. But I will draw attention to the fact that it is not usual for the House to reverse the Railway Committee's decision in a matter which was referred to it and which it has taken the trouble to carefully consider. It is a matter of discretion in every such case as to what time shall be allowed.
I do not agree with those who say that we create a precedent by our action on one such Bill, for in the very nature of things each case must stand upon its own merits.
I do not object to the Bill standing over, but I hope it will not come up on Monday, as I fear it will be impossible for me to be here on that day. [DOT]
Why not refer it back to the the committee according to the usual custom.

I do not think that
would be fair to the committee.

I understood the mover
to say that the promoters objected to the change. Perhaps it was made for good reasons, and I am sure the committee would be glad to hear them.

It was thought that
the company was trifling, as it were, with certain townsites and entrances, and that that should be stopped by making the com' pany hurry up and complete the line if they intend to do so. I do not pretend to be a judge of the matter, but the discussion in

the committee was carried on by gentlemen from the locality, and others. I myself did not vote, but after a full discussion of the matter, the amendment was carried by a vote of 22 to 10. I think it would be a reflection upon the committee to refer the Bill back unless some good reason be shown that the committee has made a mistake.

The principal reason
why the amendment was adopted was that settlers in western Canada, particularly in Alberta, have claimed that charters were given to certain companies to build railways and that no steps were taken to complete their construction, and believing that the railway was to be completed settlers took up land along the line. The minister, who has received a great many letters in connection with the matter, was willing that an amendment should be put in limiting the time within when the work must be started to one year and providing for the completion within three years. However, the main reason for the amendment is the demand of the settlers that when a railway charter is granted the construction of the line should be rushed tO' completion within a reasonable time. If they are held down to one year within which to start the promoters absolutely refuse to go on with the line.

It would be well for the committee to understand a few of the facts in connection with the work that has been carried on in Alberta during the past year. Tim proposed branch line of the Canadian Pacific railway runs into the new oil region south of Calgary. This is a very important territory, into which many people are desirous of going, and there is a tremendous rush of all kinds of freight into that section of the country. Apparently the committee got the impression that the company was not doing its duty in the province of Alberta during the past year. In order to show the committtee that the railway company is alive to all these things, I wish to quote a few statistics to show what has *been done during the past year in the province of Alberta. Last year 235 miles of grading was done by this road, 115'9 miles of track laid, and 113-4 miles ballasted. A railway company that has built 250 miles of solid track within a year cannot be accused of not having attended to its work. There are no less than six different branches from the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway under construction there now. In the beginning of the session the Railway Committee generally gets up in the air a little about railway

lines not being carried out as rapidly as they should be-as the United States phraseology has it, they get a little bull-moosed-but when the committee gets down to business, it fixes the time for starting at two years. I do not think any interest is injured by making the time two years, but if it remains one year -and the Bill is withdrawn, the people dm that section of the country will suffer, because the Canadian Pacific railway have the money to build the road and it will take them a year and a half to build it. They cannot do it in a year. I would urge strongly upon the committee that the change be-made.

In view of the fact that the committee gave this matter consideration and carried the Bill by a large majority, perhaps it would be better to let the Bill stand for the present. If this committee has to decide the matter, let it be decided when there is a larger attendance than there is to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: There is probably a good deal to be said on both sides of the matter. As I understand the facts, other similar Bills have been treated differently. At the same time, I am one of those who think one year is quite enough time for any railway company to be allowed the advantages and privileges given them by this Parliament. I do not think it would be well, perhaps, to single out one particular line [DOT]and provide different treatment for it from that which you provide for others. I agree with my hon. friend that we should let the Bill stand until we have more members present, which perhaps will be when next time Private Bills are called.

I can bear out what the hon. member for North Simcoe has said with regard to the work of the Canadian Pacific railway in Alberta this year. In my constituency they have been constructing three very important branch lines.
I do not think this amendment was aimed particularly at the Canadian Pacific railway; its object was to induce railways to complete the lines which they have had charters for for some time. Because of the frequency with which some of these companies come back to the House and ask for renewals of charters, the people are becoming discouraged and discontented in view of the possibility that the lines are not to be built for a good many years.
I can give you an instance in my own [DOT]constituency. A railway company got a charter for the construction of a branch

line, and as there was a large homestead tract of country there, the people at once flocked in. The charter has been renewed several times, the people have been there for several years, some of them being 70 miles away from a railroad. The idea of those who supported this amendment in the committee was, if possible, to limit the time [DOT] of starting and completing these lines, and letting the railways know that this Parliament is serious in its efforts to expedite railroad construction. I cannot say whether or not this will expedite construction, but, if we can show those railway companies who are coming to Parliament time after time for extensions that we are in earnest and that we want them to take active 'Steps in connection with the construction of lines for which charters have been renewed, four, five or six times, I think we should do so. The Canadian Pacific railway is the only railroad, in my part of the country, and they have been doing a lot to serve that portion of western Canada. Other railroad companies, the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific, who have charters for the construction of lines in different parts of that country, are not building their lines. 'Once a railroad obtains a charter for the construction of a line in a certain district, it is difficult to get another railroad to go into the same district. The Canadian Pacific railway was asked to build a branch line in one district and they answered that the Canadian Northern railway had a line under charter there, and it would not be worth their while to go in. I offer these observations to give some idea of the reason why this amendment was put in at the suggestion of certain members from western Canada. The particular question is a live one in my section of Alberta. The Boards of Trade are all behind the movement to secure some legislation by which this Parliament will not continually give renewals to railroads without some guarantee that they will immediately commence construction and try and rush the lines to completion as soon as possible.
Progress reported.

speechtext: House in Committee on Bill No. 13, to incorporate the Central Canada Railway Company.-Mr. W. H. Sharpe.

This is an ordinary
act of incorporation. We recommend that in order not to conflict with another railway the House change the name to the Central Western Canada Railway Company. In section 3 the capital stock has been made $7,000,000 instead of $5,000,000. In section 12 we use the expression ' approval ' instead of ' order' of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
What is the geographical location of the charter, approximately?

From Winnipeg in a northwesterly direction by way of York-

ton, Saskatoon, and Battleford to the city of Edmonton.

That route would closely parallel throughout the present connection between Winnipeg and Edmonton, via the Canadian Pacific railway and, at no great distance, the lines of the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk. Was that considered in the committee?

It was mentioned by somebody, but the committee takes the view that you cannot refuse to let a dozen lines parallel each other if they want to. We cannot force a railway to build in some place where it does not want to build, and we do not consider that we would do any harm in granting wholesale charters between points.

I was given to understand that the Minister ;of Railways .made a statement in connection with this charter, and as the minister is not here I would be very glad if we could have the statement repeated so as to have on record the policy of the Government in regard to lines paralleling each other.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Does my hon. friend object to the Bill going on?

Not at all, I am merely asking for as much information as possible while the Bill is before the committee. I may say that the recent occurrences at Quebec will, I think, satisfy every member of the House that it is not desirable to let private legislation go through without letting the members know what it is.

It has been the policy,
openly expressed in the Railway Committee for six years at least, that there shall be free trade in railway charters. That is, if a man wants a charter in any district he can get it, and if another man wants a charter over the very same ground he can get it. That has always been the policy of the committee since I have been a member of it, so there is no use in talking of detectaphones, or the deaf and dumb alphabet, or any dodges of that kind.

Like my hon. friend (Mr. Currie), I am a member of the Railway Committee, and while the general policy of free trade in railway charters has undoubtedly been agreed upon by the members of the committee, free trade in charters where lines of railway have already been built, has never been agreed upon to my knowledge. That is a new doctrine to me,

Where railroads have not been built in a district for which a railway company has a charter, there is no objection raised in the Railway Committee to somebody else getting a charter for the same territory; but if the line has already been built there surely should be some announcement of policy by the minister as to whether somebody else can come along and parallel that line for hundreds and hundreds of miles, perhaps within half a mile or a mile. That policy, I say, has never been agreed to by the Railway Committee. As I understand the request of the member for Edmonton he is asking for some statement by the Minister of Railways, or in his absence by some member of the Government, as to the policy of the Government in regard to parallel lines: whether or not the Government proposes to let this company-if the charter goes through, as no doubt it will-[DOT] parallel the present lines already covering this territory, in such close proximity that the people will not be better served, and the only result of which will be competition that would be destructive to the line already built, and of no particular benefit to the public.
Is the hon. gentleman opposed to competition among railways?

Not at all, but I am opposed to the idea of letting the railway companies spend money in building unnecessary lines, when there is such an enormous demand throughout the West, and East too, for lines that are absolutely needed to serve the public. So far as competition among the railroads is concerned, of course we want competition; but we do not want the kind of competition that will not be of any benefit to the people, and that will only be destructive of the welfare of lines already built.

Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question for my information and guidance? Would he say that when a railway asks to parallel another, that we should refuse a charter? We have either to grant it or refuse it, but we cannot grant it, and say: You must go where you have no intention of going. Will the hon. gentleman say that the committee should refuse that charter be-cause it seeks to parallel another line?

The Chairman of the Railway Committee compliments me by asking for my advice on this point- I am looking

to the chairman myself for light and information.
Don't I need it, also ?

I have no objection whatever to the granting of this charter. I should think that the Chairman of the Railway Committee ought to be sufficiently in the confidence of the Minister of Railways-they sit side by side in the committee-to tell us what the policy of the minister will be when, having granted this charter, as I have no doubt this committee intends to do, the railway proposes to parallel the line already constructed.

I may tell my hon.
friend that I am not in any such confidence, nor do I think I should be. I am simply Chairman of the Railway Committee. I cannot tell any better than the hon. gentle-* man himself what the particular policy of the Minister of Railways is in this regard, nor do I think I ought to assume that I am sufficiently in the confidence of the Minister of Railways, to have the right to ask him. I do not pretend to be anything but Chairman of the Committee representing the Parliament in that committee-not the Government, not the Opposition, not the supporters of the Government, but the whole of this House of Parliament, and the committee has to take the responsibility. And with all deference to my hon. friend, I do not think it is a matter that the Government should have a policy upon. I think it is a matter for this parliamentary committee to settle. In some parts of Ontario we would like to see the railways paralleled. In my own district there is a railway that cannot begin to do the work and we need a parallel line badly. We need competition and extra facilities. I could name many instances where it is absolutely necessary in the public interest to get more than one railway between the same cities, practically paralleling each other. But what I want to ask my hon. friend is whether he individually thinks that we ought to go to the length of saying to a railway company : be-beeause you are paralleling another line we shall not give you a charter. I do not know that we have the right to ask for the confidence of any minister to guide us in the committee, so long as we act pursuant to the Railway Act.

I accept the position taken by my hon. friend, 'that he is Chairman of the Railway Committee for this whole House. But at the same time I say that 49
when this Bill leaves the Railway Committee and comes before this House we are entitled to a pronouncement by the Minister of Railways as to what his policy is, when it comes to a question of giving or withholding his consent when the final plans of the promoters of a Bill are brought before him for his consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If there is any objection to the Bill we will be very glad to let it stand until some future time.

Perhaps ft would be just as well. There are other Bills on the list that would not be contentious, but this is a yery important Bill, and to my mind raises a very important question.
