When the committee rose at six o'clock, I stated that the lightkeeper, Mr. Marin Bourque, was so ill at the date fixed for the second investigation to be held on the charge of partisanship preferred against him that he was unable to appear before Mr. Duchemin. I have here a statutory declaration signed by his wife verifying the facts. It reads:
In the matter of dismissal of Marin Bourque, keeper of the lighthouse at River Bourgeois, Richmond county, N.S.
I,	Catherine Bourque of River Bourgeois in the county of Richmond do solemnly declare that I am the wife of Marin Bourque ate keeper of the lighthouse at River Bourgeois. That my husband received a notice from H. P. Duchemin, commissioner, on the evening of December 11, 1912, to appear before him in the office of William Dorscoute at River Bourgeois for the investigation of charges of political partisanship against him on December 12, 1912.
That at the time my husband received this notice he was confined to his bed by illness and was unable to attend the investigation.
That I went to see Mr. Duchemin at the office of Mr. Dorscoute on December 12, and told him that my husband could not leave his bed and was therefore unable to appear before him.
That Mr. Duchemin. then told me he wanted my husband to make a statement to him in regard to the charge of political partisanship preferred against him. He said that at the previous investigation my husband was prevented from making a statement by Mr. Kyte, M.P., and Dr. Bissett, M.P.P.
I then told him that my husband had already made a statement under oath which had been sent to Ottawa. Mr. Duchemin said he wanted a statement made to him as he was appointed for that purpose. Mr. Duchemin did not tell me that there were any witnesses to be examined against my husband but he said he came for the purpose of getting a statement from my husband. And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.

him. Mr. Duchemin has cost the country enough money without sending him to cover the same ground twice, merely to enable him to ferret out, if possible, testimony to support the charges made against an official by those who are anxious to get his position for their friend. On the occasion of the second inquiry, which was ordered by the minister to take place at Eiver Bourgeois on December 12, Mr. Bourque was too ill to appear before the commissioner. His wife was there, however, and Mr. Duchemin told her that he came there for the purpose of getting a statement from her husband. . As her husband was too ill to attend, he could get no statement from him. After Mrs. Bourque left the office of Mr. Levisconte, Mr. Duchemin did hold an inquiry and did examine witnesses into the allegations of partisanship made against Mr. Bourque. If Mr. Duchemin was desirous of acting in good faith, he would at least have told Mr. Bourque's wife that he would examine any witnesses who might be brought before him, and that such evidence as he was able to procure would be forwarded to Ottawa. But he made no such assertion, rather intimating to her that he came merely for the purpose of taking a statement from Mr. Bourque himself. I have here a copy of the report of the second investigation made by Mr. Duchemin, which is as follows:
Sydney, N.S., Dec. 16, 1912. Hon. J. D. Hazen, M.P.,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:
. On the 12th instant, I took evidence at River Bourgeois, in the matter of Marin Bourque,
formerly lightkeeper at that place.
Mr. Bourque was duly notified of the time and place of the hearing, hut was not present. His wife, however, came before the beginning Of the inquiry, and stated that her husband was not feeling well enough to be present, but that, in any case, he wished to tell me he did not intend to appear, as he had nothing further to say in addition to the statement already sent forward. I advised her that any statement he had previously sent forward to the department would be of no avail at this investigation, and it would be necessary for him to come personally before me if he wished to have any statements sent forward to the department. I further advised her that he might appear either during the inquiry, or at any time before X left River Bourgeois, that I would submit to him the evidence taken, and would be pleased to transmit to the department any statement he might wish to make. She again assured me, however, that he would not appear, and as a matter of fact Mr. Bourque did not appear before me either during the inquiry or thereafter.
The reason why he did not appear, as is

set forth in Mrs. Bourque's declaration, was because he was too ill to attend. Mr. Duchemin proceeds:
Testimony was given by Wm. J. Levisconte, merchant, of River Bourgeois, and Wm. Boudreau, master mariner, of the same place.
Mr. Levisconte testified that he had been doing business at River Bourgeois for about twenty-one years, and that he knew everybody living in the district. He added that he had always taken an active interest in political matters on the Conservative side, and was well acquainted with the political workers on both sides of politics; that he had known Mr. Bourque for years, and declared that he had for years been a most objectionable Liberal partisan. Mr. Levisconte said : ' In the Dominion election of 1908, when the campaign was in progress, Marin Bourque used most objectionable language towards the Conservatives. He spoke of them as " that dirty party." '
A few moments ago I read the evidence given by Levisconte in the inquiry of September 25, and these are the exact words that he used. But, when pressed by Mr. Duchemin to say when Bourque used that language attributed to him, he was unable to do so, and became very angry because Mr. Duchemin insisted that he should tell at what election that language was used. However, at the second inquiry, if Mr. Duchemin's report be true, Mr. Levisconte had refreshed his memory and was able to say that the language was used in the election of 1908.
He said: T would never vote for that 'dirty party'. He said this to me here in River Bourgeois.' Mr. Levisconte added that while Marin Bourque was not a man who exercised much influence in the district, he had neverthless always been offensive and objectionable as a Liberal partisan.
Wm. Boudreau testified that Mr. Bourque had been in the habit of talking politics openly In a nasty and insulting way. Witness said: 'In the 1908 elections I was working In the interests of Mr. Ferguson, the Conservative candidate. A few days before the election Mr. Bourque said I was a fool to he working for that party (the Conservative party) because they were going to be licked anyway. Mr. Boudreau corroborated the statement of Mr. Levisconte-that while Marin Bourque was never in a position to do much for his party, that he had always been openly offensive when elections were taking place.
I therefore find that Marin Bourque has been an offensive partisan, and that on this ground the department was warranted in dispensing with his services.
In the investigation held in the month of September, at which I was present for the purpose of taking a record of the proceedings, Mr. Levisconte was not in a position to furnish any evidence that could be considered sufficient to support the charge made against Mr. Bourque. In my presence Mr. Duchemin said that there was no

evidence upon which the dismissal of Mr. Bourque could be justified. In the second inquiry that took place in December, the same witness was examined and the evidence given was exactly the same, except in so far as the witness is alleged to have said that the language referred to was used in the election of 1908. Wm. Boudreau, the other witness, did not pretend to say in what particular Mr. Bourque was an offensive partisan, or in what instances he had canvassed or worked for the Liberal party; he merely said, in a general way, that Mr. Bourque was an offensive partisan. The point I desire to make is that, Levisconte, having failed to furnish evidence against Mr. Bourque in the inquiry which took place in September, and no other evidence having been subsequently adduced to justify the minister in dismissing this man, he should have been reinstated without an instant's delay. There was no justification for the department going to the expense of holding a second inquiry, particularly in view of the fact that the important witness was the same person who gave evidence in September. I need scarcely remind the committee that where a witness is called to give testimony in a certain case, and on [DOT] another occasion goes upon the witness stand in the same case and tells the court another story, his evidence is always regarded with a good deal of suspicion. As I stated, Bourque was in ill health when he was dismissed from the lighthouse. He continued to be in ill health, and, if it is any satisfaction to the minister to know it, Bourque is not in a position, nor never will be in a position in the flesh, to rise up and condemn him for his conduct; he died a few months ago. His case is an extremely sad one. His death was no doubt accelerated by the treatment he received at the hands of Mr. Duchemin and at the hands of the Minister of Marine. This man Bourque was not a partisan in any sense of the word. He was a man without language to express his ideas in any matter outside of his own particular duty. He took so little interest in politics that he voted but once, I believe, since he was appointed to the lighthouse. He never attended a political meeting, notwithstanding the statement of Mr. Gillies, the defeated Conservative- candidate, that he was an open, violent partisan, went to public meetings, canvassed openly, took voters to the poll, and did everything that constituted offensive partisanship. It is very strange that, when an inquiry took place,
his neighbour, Mr. Wm. J. Levisconte, who knew him for twenty-one years, was called, but could not testify that Bourque had ever canvassed anybody or attended public meetings or hauled a voter to the poll. All he could say was that this man told him once that he would not vote for his dirty party. He would not undertake to say at what election he made, that statement, but, if he made the statement, it was fair to assume that it was before he was appointed to the office of light-keeper, because we have the declaration of Bourque that ever since he bad been appointed lighthouse keeper he had never attended a public meeting or taken any part in politics, and bad never committed any offence which would justify dismissal. I would like to know if there is to be finality to these investigations. Ordinarily, when a charge is made, the accused is put on trial, the evidence is all put in, and the charge dismissed or sustained and the case closed for all time. As regards the poor official, he never knows when he is going to be at rest. An investigation may be called this month, and if no evidence is produced against him, there may be another one next month or a month after. But once Nemesis, in the shape of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, is on the trail of an official in his department, there is to be no rest or contentment for that man; he must go sooner or later, whether the facts and circumstances justify his dismissal or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member for Richmond has discussed this matter at very considerable length, and has read the different papers and reports that are in possession of the Marine and Fisheries Department bearing on this subject. As the hon. gentleman's object was no doubt to get these papers and reports embalmed on the records of ' Hansard,' his purpose is accomplished. What are the facts as they present themselves to the department and as they present themselves from a careful perusal of the reports and documents received ? The facts are, that Joseph A. Gillies, a former member of this House of Commons, a gentleman very highly respected in the community in which he lives, and a candidate in the last election at Richmond, reported to the department that this man Bourque had, to his own personal knowledge, been guilty of active partisanship, reciting the details of the partisanship and asking for his dismissal. I cannot

bring myself to believe for one single minute, knowing Mr. Gillies as I do, that Mr. Gillies would take the responsibility of making an accusation saying he did it from personal knowledge of the facts, if he did not have personal knowledge of the facts and was not sure of his ground. On Mr. Gillies' recommendation, it was decided to dismiss Bourque from his position as lightkeeper; but, yielding to the request of the hon. member for Richmond, I ordered an investigation to be held, and the matter was placed in the hands of Mr. Duchemin, who was conducting investigations into matters of offensive partisanship in the eastern part of Nova Scotia. Mr. Duchemin reported to the department that he had decided to hold an investigation on the 27th of September, that notice had been sent to Mr. Bourque and to the complainant, that Bourque had appeared, but no witnesses had appeared to give testimony against him. Bourque declined to be sworn or to make any statement under oath to be transmitted to the department. There is the report received from Mr. Duchemin, that no witnesses appeared to testify and Bourque declined to be sworn or to make any statement that could be sent to the department. Now, the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) says that is not a true statement of what took place. It is a statement given in the solemn report of the commissioner to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and the only statement regarding the matter that I have before me; and not one single statement to the contrary effect was ever made to me until I heard it here to-day by the hon. member for Richmond. It was represented to me that there was a mistake, that witnesses were prepared to attend and give evidence that Bourque was a notorious partisan and an active worker in the Liberal interests; and in consequence of that Mr. Duchemin was instructed to take up the matter, to notify Bourque and the complainant and get the evidence on both sides. Mr. Duchemin, having received those instructions, reported to the department that Bourque was duly notified of the time and place of hearing; but was not present; that his wife came before the beginning of the inquiry and stated her husband was not feeling well enough to be present, but that in any case he did not intend to appear as he had nothing further to say in addition to the statement already sent forward.
I wrote to the hon. member for Richmond and told him that if Bourque would state
IMr. Hazen.]
that he had not taken part in elections I would order an investigation to be held. Therefore we have the statement of Mr. Duchemin to the effect that Bourque's wife appeared before him and said he did not intend to appear before him and in any circumstance he had made a statement that had been sent to the department. Mr. Duchemin says:
I advised her that any statement he had previously sent forward to the department would he of no avail with this investigation, and it would be necessary for him to come personally before me if he wished to have any statement sent forward to the department. X further advised her that he might appear either during the inquiry or at any time before I left River Bourgeois and that I would be pleased to transmit to the department any statements he might wish to make.
According to that report of Mr. Duchemin, every opportunity was given to Bourque to reply to the evidence that was to be given at that investigation. He made no attempt to do so and had he represented to Mr. Duchemin that he would give on a later date a reply to the evidence given at that investigation, I have not the slightest doubt that every opportunity would have been afforded him to do so. But on the contrary he did not do so, and we have the statement of the commission that his wife told him he did not intend to appear anyway because he relied upon the statement he had previously made and which had been filed with the department. The commissioner went on to take the evidence and made his report. Three witnesses were examined and this is the report:
Mr. Levisconte whom I understand is a native of River Bourgeois testified that he had being doing business at River Bourgeois for about twenty-one years and that he knew everybody living in the district. He added that he had always taken an active interest in political matters on the Conservative side and was well acquainted with the political workers on both sides of politics; that he had known Bourque for years and declared he had been for years a most objectionable partisan.
Mr. Levisconte said: 'In the Dominion election of 1908, when the campaign was in progress, Marin Bourque used most objectionable language toward the Conservative. He spoke of them as 'that dirty party.' He said: 'I would never vote for that dirty party'. He said this to me here in River Bourgeois. Mr. Levisconte added that while Marin Bourque was not a man who exercised much influence in the district, he had nevertheless always been offensive and objectionable as a Liberal partisan.
Aaiother witness appeared and gave evidence. Mr. Boudreau testified:
That Mr. Bourque had been in the habit of 'talking politics openly in a nasty and insulting way.' Witness said: 'In the 1908 election, I was

working in the interests of Mr. Ferguson, the Conservative candidate. A few days before the election, Mr. Bourque said, *1 was a fool to he working for that party (the Conservative party) because they were going to get licked anyway/
If that is not canvassing and trying to influence voters in an election I would like to know what is.
Mr. Boudreau corroborated the statement of Mr. Bevisconte that while Marin Bourque was never in a position to do much for his party, that he had always been openly offensive when elections were taking place.
Mr. Bourque had an opportunity of appearing at the investigation, or at any time later on when the commissioner was in River Bourgeois, to give evidence and deny the truth of the statements made against him but he did not choose to do so, and I say it is no wonder therefore that the commissioner concludes his report by saying:
I therefore find that Marin Bourque has been an offensive partisan and that on this ground the department was warranted in dispensing with his services.
These are the facts as they appear on the files of t'he department. The hon. member for Richmond asked me to accept his statement to the effect that Duchemin has acted in a most dishonest and outrageous manner: that he has made statements that are not true, to the department; that he has deceived the department and that the statements contained in his report are false and untrue. I fail to understand what purpose Mr. Duohemin could have in doing anything of that sort. He was acting under a commission from the Government under the Enquiries Act, and what purpose he could have had in making a report to the department that was not true, is something which I entirely fail to understand, and 1 will not accept that as being true in regard to Mr. Duchemin, unless absolute evidence is given of that fact. Mr. Duchemin has been accused by my hon. friend from Richmond. He is not here to defend himself, and I want to say to my hon. friend from Richmond that I will accept that report of Mr. Duchemin until the contrary is shown to be true, for I cannot believe that any responsible man, as I believe Mr. Duchemin to be, would take the course of making false statements regarding evidence given before him, when the making of those false statements would injure a man, who in the opinion of my hon. friend from Richmond, was innocent of the charges made against him. The facts are all there and quite clear. If the facts contained in that report of Mr. Duchemin are true, there is no doubt whatever that this man was a partisan, and a most objectionable partisan, and under the rule laid down by this House some years ago, he had no reason to find fault because of his dismissal from office.

If this was the first time
we had heard of Mr. DucheminJs conduct in the province of Nova Scotia, my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries might more successfully put on an air of seeming offence at the challenge offered as to the character of his commissioner. Does the hon. minister forget that in the last session of Parliament a case was brought by me to his attention where he summoned Michael O'Brien, keeper of the light of Bear Island, to appear" before him at Port Malcolm to answer certain charges. Mr. Duchemin held the court at Port Hawkesbury, nine miles away, so that it was impossible for O'Brien to attend to answer the charges. It may become the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to have a defective memory to-night, because it is not convenient to remember all the facts and circumstances brought to his attention with regard to his blessed commissioner down in Cape Breton. Does the hon. minister not know that it was brought to the attention of the House, that notwithstanding Mr. Duchemin was directed to allow counsel to appear for the accused, he absolutely refused to hear counsel and took the conduct of the case entirely in his own hands. Mr. Duchemin in his second report to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries does not state that he told Mrs. Bourque that it was his intention to summon other witnesses to give testimony against her husband. He simply said:	I come here
for the purpose of getting a statement from your husband, inasmuch as no statement has been made by him that I can forward to Ottawa. Had Mr. Duchemin told Mrs. Bourque: ' there are two witnesses who are prepared to give evidence against you,' and if in face of the knowledge of that fact Bourque had shown indifference to his interest and refused to attend the inquiry, then the Minister of Marine might have some semblance of excuse for the conduct of Duchemin in this respect. Mr. Bourque knew that at the investigation held in the month of September no evidence was given against him, and that no evidence could be given against him in that regard. He knew he was not obliged to give evidence in reply to a charge that had not been proved against

him, and inasmuch as his statement made on oath was in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, did he not do what any sane man would have done under the circumstances when he said: As there is no evidence against me, there is nothing for me to answer and my statement stands in the office of the Department of Marine at the present time. There is the whole case. The Minister of Marine says that Bourque had an opportunity of appearing before Duchemin. Opportunity to appear for what purpose? He appeared before him in the month of September. Mr. Levisconte, the star witness, was called and his evidence was so ridiculous, so defective, and fell so far short of. proving the charge against Bourque, that even Duchemin, in view of my presence and the presence of others there, would not undertake to report that evidence was given against him sufficient to justify his dismissal. But I state that Duchemin sent a deceptive report to the Minister of Marine, for which, of course, I do not hold the minister responsible, because I aver again that Levisconte was called -and was examined by Duchemin, and having failed to give evidence to implicate the accused as regards the charges made against him, Mr. Duchemin was obliged to drop the case. After I made the inquiry as to whether or not the lightkeeper was to be reinstated, 1 found that a second inquiry was ordered by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. When I heard that I addressed a letter to the minister expressing my astonishment.
, The letter is dated December 16, 1912, and reads as follows:
Hon. J. D. Hazen,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-With reference to the dismissal of Marin Bourque, lightkeeper at River Bourgeois, who was dismissed in the month of April last; You are aware that an investigation was held into the charges of partisanship made 'against him, before Mr. Duchemin on the 26th day of September, last.
I am very much surprised to learn that Mr. Bourque was again summoned to appear before Duchemin for investigation on the 12th of December instant, to answer to the same charges. I cannot believe that Mr. Duchemin had authority from you to institute the second inquiry, and I would be obliged if you will inform me whether or not he was so instructed.
To which letter I received the following reply:
Office of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of Canada,
Ottawa, December 18, 1912.
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of yours of the 16 th instant expressing surprise that further

investigation was held into charges preferred against Mr. Marin Bourque, keeper of the light at River Bourgeois.
In reply I have to inform you that subsequent to the receipt of a report from Mr. Duchemin, barrister, Sydney, N.S., who was instructed to examine into the charges of partisanship preferred against Mr. Bourque, verbal representations were made to me to the effect that testimony was available to prove the allegations made against Mr. Bourque, and that further opportunity should be offered for its production.
After carefully considering the matter, 1 decided to re-open it and instructed Mr. Duchemin to arrange for a rehearing at River Bourgeois at his early convenience, serving all interested parties with notice of the time and place of inquiry. I am awaiting Mr. Duche-min's report.
Yours faithfully,
J. D. Hazen.
I am curious to know from what source the minister received this verbal information. Perhaps he would not mind stating to me now who was the person who gave the information to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One of them was Mr. Gillies, and I think there were others.

Mr. Gillies is the gentleman who made the statement in the beginning that this man Bourque was a partisan, a man against whom not a single tittle of evidence could be produced by men who had known him for twenty years. Mr. Gillies lives in the city of Sydney, almost 100 miles from where Mr. Bourque resided. He does not visit the county of Richmond except when an election campaign is on and how could Mr. Gillies be in possession of certain facts of an intimate character that his friend, Mr. Levisconte, did not know about although he had lived for twenty years within gunshot of Mr. Bourque himself?
The name of Mr. Gillies is not heard in
this House to-night for the first time. I will refrain from making a reply to the compliment that the minister paid him this evening for the reason that Mr. Gillies is not present and is therefore not able to defend himself. But it is within the recollection of the members of this committee that certain facts and circumstances were brought before the attention of this House last year which do not reflect very much to the credit of Mr. Gillies and do not contribute very much to the credit of the minister himself who acted upon the recommendations which Mr. Gillies made to him. One of the most serious allegations brought against any member of this Government was made during the last session of Parliament by myself in respect to the release

from jail of a man who had been tried and committed for forgery, in order that he might enjoy the emoluments of public office conferred upon him by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on a recommendation that was made by Mr. Gillies. In view of the fact that the minister is able to stand up to-day without a blush upon his countenance and speak of the high character of Mr. Gillies, and justify himself in accepting his recommendation, I have very little hope that the minister will alter the fatuous course he has pursued with regard to taking Mr. Gillies to his political and personal bosom as he has done heretofore.

The discussion in regard to our old friend, Mr. Duchemin, makes it necessary for me to make a correction in a statement of the hon Minister of Marine and Fisheries appearing in ' Hansard ' a few days ago in regard to the money that is being paid to this executioner in the province of Nova Scotia for cutting off the heads of decent people. I made inquiries last year in regard to the large sums that were paid to this gentleman for the very unfair and disreputable work that he has been hired to do in that province, and the Government were kind enough to give me a pretty full return. The other day I wanted to pursue this inquiry a little further and obtain additional particulars as to the amount of money paid to Mr. Duchemin since the time at which the previous report was placed on the table, the 21st May, 1913. I accordingly framed a new series of questions for that purpose. My first question is:
1. What was the gross amount paid by all departments of the Government to H. P. Duchemin, commissioner, from the date of his appointment to December 31, 1913, for his services in connection with investigations of partisanship, including travelling and living expenses?
The minister undertakes to answer that question, and this is his answer as it appears in ' Hansard ':
Mr. Hazen:	1. $1,664.85.
I submit that this answer is incorrect, and I assume that the mistake arises from the minister referring only to his own department and not to all the departments of Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That answer, of course,
should have gone to the Secretary of State.

It was produced in the House by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The answer was handed to the clerk and it appears in ' Hansard ' as the answer from all the departments of the Government. The answer I got last year from the various departments of the Government who made answer was-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman
tell me what page of ' Hansard ' that is on?

I think it was yesterday or the day before. It was quite recently. I was pointing out that last year, on the 21st May, when I made this inquiry in regard to the money paid to this gentleman, by all the departments of the Government I got the following reply:
Post Office Department, $1,053.78; Railways and Canals, $1,850.15 ; Marine and Fisheries, $1,691.10.
You will note, Mr. Chairman, that the sum paid by the Department of Marine and Fisheries last year was larger than the sum that the hon. minister tells me now was paid by all the departments of Government since the appointment of Mr. Duchemin.
Department of Public Works, $389.48; Department of Customs, $1,190.66; Department of Agriculture, $124.66.
Making a total paid to Mr. Duchemin of $6,299.77 up to the 21st day of May, 1913. In addition to that certain sundries were charged up by this gentleman and paid by the various departments amounting to the sum of $697.21. It is clear, therefore, that there must be some error in the return that has been given to me by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is perfectly clear what that error was. These answers are all prepared in the departments and sent to the Department of the Secretary of State which is the collecting department. The Secretary of State has to answer general questions of this sort addressed to the Government, the answers to which have to come from the several departments. This answer should have been handed to the Secretary of State, but evidently, through some mistake, it has been sent to me here in the House by an official of the department, and I have handed it in as the answer to the question. Instead of that, it should have gone to the Secretary of State and he should have collected the answers from the different departments and totalled the amounts up altogether.

Will the minister see
that this is corrected and that a full and accurate report is given to the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. I think that ought to be struck out of ' Hansard ' because it gives an entirely incorrect impression. The question ought to be answered by the Secretary of State giving the full information after having collected it from the different departments which have used the services of Mr. Duchemin as a commissioner. I do not know whether it can be struck out of ' Hansard ' now or not, but I will consult with Mr. Speaker and see what can be done.

Will the minister
explain to me how it was that on the 21st May, 1913, his department reported to the House that $1,691.10 had been paid for expenses to Mr. Duchemin. It also appears by the answers I have just referred to that Mr. Duchemin did additional work during the current year since the date of the answers. The amount which is now stated is less, namely $1,664.85. Can the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot explain it at the moment. I will have to find out at the department. I do not prepare these answers. They are prepared by the accountant of the department. Will the hon. gentleman let me get the facts? The question was:
What was the gross amount paid by all departments of the Government to H. P. Duchemin, commissioner, from the date of his appointment to December 31, 1913, for his services in connection with investigations of partisanship, including travelling and living expenses?
And the answer given is:

You say that the answer given last year conflicts with this?
The amount on the 21st of May, 1913, was stated as $1,961.10.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What question is that in answer to?

I have not the question, but you will find it in ' Hansard ' of the 21st of May, 1913. There will also be an error in the number of investigations or the number of parties whose dismissal Mr. Duchemin recommended. The question is, ' How many dismissals of officials did the said Mr. Duchemin recommend in all the departments?' The answer is ' sixty-seven,' which of course is incorrect, as well as the amount of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That refers to the Department of Marine and Fisheries only.

I thought that last year, after all the information that we had laid before the minister in regard to this gentleman, Mr. Duchemin, that my hon. friend would have made some investigation in regard to Mr. Duchemin's character, and that he would not come before the House at this date and say that he would give him the benefit of the doubt in regard to the conduct of investigations. Mr. Duchemin violated the law in many particulars, which were pointed out to my hon. friend and the other members of the Government at the last session of Parliament. Everybody knows that under the Investigation Act, every official has the right to be represented by counsel. It is the common right of every British subject. I do not care what the charge against a man is, it may be murder, treason, or any capital charge, but it has always been recognized in every British court that a man charged with any kind of crime has the right to be represented by counsel. This was so apparent to everybody that the Prime Minister insisted on placing it in the Investigation Act, and some of his friends had headlines placed in the newspapers showing what a magnanimous gentleman the Prime Minister was that he would give those poor Grit officials who were being charged with partisanship the right to be represented by counsel. This must have been known to Mr. Duchemin, because he is a lawyer; and if he had not read the Investigation Act, certainly he was not fit for the position in which my hon. friend had placed him. I am not charging Mr. Duchemin with anything that I cannot prove. If my hon. friend requires any proof, 1 can give it to him from the mouth of Mr. Duchemin himself. If my hon. friend will refer to a return that was placed before the House last year, in regard to the dismissal of Mr. R. Conroy, postmaster at Country Harbour, N.S., he will find the following language from Mr. Duchemin's report. Mr. Duchemin says:
Mr. Floyd, who is, I understand, a solicitor in the town,-
that is, the town of Guysborough

-asked if he might represent one of the accused at the hearing. I declined to allow him to act, herein following the precedent laid down by Mr. J. T. Ross, the commissioner appointed in 1896-7, to do similar work. I had months before declined to hear counsel on the ground that it would unduly prolong these hearings and would involve very great delay in reaching the many cases that had to be taken up.
There were so many people who had to have their heads cut off that Mr. Duchemin could not be bothered going into the de-

tails to see whether a man was guilty or not. What he considered to be his duty was to go along as fast as possible and to do this work without finding out whether there was a defence or not. He goes on to say:
My attitude in this regard was subsequently confirmed by the department for which I was carrying on the inquiry.
I do not know whether that is true or not. On several occasions I have tried to find out what department that was. I have a question on the Order Paper now, and I trust my hon. friend will be able to give me that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The question on the Order Paper is not addressed to me.

Mr. Duchemin, whom
my hon. friend represents here to-night as being a fit official to conduct investigations, makes the statement that some department of this Government instructed him not to allow counsel to be present at these hearings. He further states that his attitude in this regard was subsequently confirmed by the department for which he was carrying on the inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He made that answer in
a letter written to me, and I instructed him to retain counsel. Therefore, it does not refer to me.

This refers to the Post Office Department, but I would like to have some department answer that question. I am addressing my speech now to the Secretary of State who represents all these departments. If a commissioner, who is appointed by an Order in Council, has been instructed by any department of the Government not to allow counsel to be employed in these investigations, I think it is our right to know which department of the Government has violated the law in that respect. I have endeavoured several times to find out which department it was, but so far I have not got any answer.
That is one instance, and Mr. Duchemin admits that for months he was travelling around the country dismissing officials, refusing them the right to be represented by counsel and practically not taking enough time over these investigations to discover whether the men were guilty or not. This is the man to whom we have paid the large sum of between $6,000 or $7,000 for doing work which it would have been far better not to have done at all. If there is anything at all worth while having in this
country, it is fair play and justice. If we could get that, we would not mind paying for it, but we do not want to be compelled to pay good money for the kind of justice that we have been getting from Mr. Duchemin. It is an imposition, and it would be much more to the credit of my hon. friend if he would dismiss these officials at once, take the heads off all these lightkeepers who were Liberals without any investigation or without anything more than simply a letter or a telegram as was done in some instances in my constituency, than that hasty investigations should be carried on and men who were innocent should be found guilty without a proper trial. There was a case of very great hardship in my constituency. It was a very small affair, but it just shows how small a great political party can be on some occasions. A man by the name of George Jollotta was employed as fishery guardian on the St. Mary's river. He had held the position for a number of years, and was a good officer. He was unfortunate in having a very severe illness which ended in the amputation of both his legs above the knee. He was therefore very much crippled, and it was only because he was a man of great pluck and perseverance that he was able to make a living at all. Everybody was pleased at the fact that Jollotta under such circumstances still kept on the struggle to make a living and did not appeal to the county to assist him. He had a very small position of fishery guardian on the St. Mary's river at a salary 'of $20 a year. He had filled the position for four or five years, and he had filled it'very well. The principal duty of an officer on that river is to watch the salmon nets and to see that the nets are not placed too far across the channel of the stream. Jollotta furnished himself with a motor boat, and was able to get up and down the river, watch the nets and do his work very well. Last year when I referred incidentally to this matter, hon. members asked me why we employed a man of that description as a fishery guardian. I want to explain to the House that he was able to do the work very well indeed. He was a faithful officer, and owing to the fact that he could get among the nets with his motor boat he could do just as well as a man who was able to use both his legs. Without an investigation Mr. Jollotta was dismissed and his position given to one of the friends of the Minister, of Marine and Fisheries. This is perhaps one of the worst cases that happened in the county I have the honour to represent. I know what the

minister's answer will be. He will say that fishery guardians are appointed not by Order in Council, but at the will of the Government, and are supposed to he appointed every year. That is true, but the minister will find, if he looks over the records, that in my constituency' at all events, the same fishery guardians have held office for many years. A man becomes accustomed to the work, and if he proves a good officer we never think of changing him. It would be a very poor excuse for taking away a little twenty-dollar job from a man like this-that the reason you took the job from him was that you had the power to do so. The story of this man is very well told in a statement which appeared in the Morning Chronicle at the time it happened:
The said- George Jollotta a few years ago was the victim of tubercular disease of the . knees, and his life was saved by having his legs amputated at the hips. By industry, frugality, and the help of friends, he was enabled to have himself fitted with a pair of artificial legs. Mr. Jollotta's family consists of his widowed mother, about 80 years old, and two children about five 'and six years old.
Nothwithstanding these infirmities, by industry and perseverance, he was able to make a living for himself and family. The $20 he received for duties as river warden was a great help to him in his struggles. He built himself a little boat in which he had a three horse-power gasoline engine installed. In this boat he performed his duties of river warden and followed his occupation, fishing.
People were glad to see this young man's energy and admired his pluck and enterprise. Any help that could be rendered him without hurting his sense of independence was always gladly given by well disposed people. Many a person in like circumstances would have given up the fight and have become a charge on the public. Not so with George Jollotta. Despite his disabilities he struggled on and made a living for himself and helpless dependents.
On September 21, 1911, a change took place. The * party of gentlemen ' came into power and they immediately cast envious eyes on the $20 job of this worthy citizen, and one of the first public acts of the great ' Imperialist,' Mr. Borden, the guarlian of the public service, was to deprive poor crippled George Jollotta of this little $20 job and give it to one of the hungry Tory office seekers-to a man in the prime of health and strength, and who rumour says had no time to attend to any of the duties of river warden, without it is, to draw the $20 salary.
So much for an example of the acts of the great ' Imperial party of gentlemen ' in this county.
I know that the minister himself is a very high-minded and honourable gentleman, which makes it all the more amazing that he should permit his supporters, for the sake of a shabby twenty dollars, to take a position away from a man who had lost both his legs. I thought, therefore, that

the case should be placed on ' Hansard ' to show how far these gentlemen will go in these matters.
My hon. friend, in his speech the other evening on the transportation of fish, boasted about what his party had done in the fish hatcheries throughout the country. I took the , trouble to look the matter -up to see if any new departure had been taken in this important matter, 'and to my amazement I found that nothing had been done except to dismiss sixteen skilled officers from the fish hatcheries and replace them with sixteen untrained men. Everybody knows that fish hatcheries must be run by skilled mein, for it takes years to learn the business. The late Government would not appoint a .man in charge of a fish hatchery, unless he had had a training in some other hatchery and understood the work. There are some branches of the public service that ought to be clearly above politics. These fish hatchery positions are small at the best. But the importance of the service should be considered. I told the minister last year and I repeat now, that the life saving service on the coast should not be regarded as political and that even if a man in charge of a life-saving station should be indiscreet enough to say a word in favour of the other side in politics, that is no reason why he should be dismissed if he is a good man. The position is so important that if the man is the right man for the position, the Government might well take the position that the lifesaving service-and -the same applies to the hatchery service-should be outside of politics. Otherwise, see what the result will be. If the Government should change next year, as we expect it will, there will be a demand for the dismissal of these sixteen men from the hatcheries and the reinstatement of the sixteen men who had been dismissed before. The same with the life saving service. And I must say, looking at it from this distance from the event, that that is the right thing to do, for I have no doubt that in many cases these dismissed officers had more experience and were better, practical men than those who succeeded them. But under this principle you could not build up good service in this or any department. These are matters which, because of their importance, I lay before the committee and call to the special attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman referred to a case in liis county of George Jollotta. I think he is hard up for material

when he brings that case before the committee. He knows that the position which Mr. Jollotta occupied is a mere temporary position and that the practice which prevails now prevailed when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office-the member for the constituency supporting the Government was asked to name parties to fill these positions. The hon. gentleman said that the same men continued to hold these offices in Guysborough year after year. So they did, probably, some of them, for about fifteen years, but that was because the same party was in power during the whole of that time. But in 1896, when the Government he supported came into office, practically every fishery guardian in Canada was dismissed and new men put in their places-or rather not dismissed, but simply not reappointed, for these are temporary employees. The hon. gentleman sheds tears over this case,-1 never heard the man's name before-yet he supported a government that treated in the same way practically every fishery overseer in Canada.
We never dismissed a man who had no legs.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I quite fail to understand how ia man who had no legs could be an efficient fishery guardian, although we would not, of course, expect a man to do very much for $20 a year. With regard to the fish hatcheries, it is the opinion of the officers of the department who have charge of that work that the fish hatcheries in Canada were never in as efficient a condition as they are at the present time. This year they are filled with eggs practically to capacity, and we expect next season to have the best results that have been obtained since we first had fish hatcheries in Canada.

I regret that I was not here the whole evening, but I have heard enough of the debate to enable me to say a word or two to my hon. friend the minister in regard to the methods in which dismissals are made in Nova Scotia through the agency of Mr. Duchemin. When my hon. friend started out to make dismissals, I am surprised that this Government did not find some better instrument for that work than this bold and ruthless gentleman, Mr. Duchemin, who is simply .a cheap partisan, possessing no qualifications whatever to carry out any judicial duties or to conduct examinations. True, he was a member of the bar, but
that is about all that can be said of him. So far as his judicial aptitude is concerned, I know of no member of the bar in the province of Nova Scotia who is less fitted than this man to perform judicial duties. Let us -consider his method of administering oaths. Does my hon. friend the minister know whether he administered oaths in -any of the inquiries which he conducted, and, if so, what kind of oaths did he administer ? Of course the minister accepted as a matter of course anything that this gentleman said. But let me tell him a little -story concerning the manner in which this exemplary judicial official administered oaths. A charge was made against -a gentleman in another department of the Government in the province of Nova Scotia, and at the inquiry a witness by the name of Currie was called to give evidence. This gentleman gave testimony which would go to indicate that the accused person should he dismissed. Immediately after the investigation was held the gentleman accused denied upon oath the assertions made by Mr. Currie, and proceeded to have him arrested for perjury. When the case came up for trial at the Supreme Court, what defence do you think Mr. Currie made? He said: 'I was not sworn at all; no legal oath was administered to me.' He asserted that Mr. Ducheimin did not administer to him the oath the law contemplates, asking him to pledge the truth of his statements. And whom did Mr. Currie call as a witness on his own behalf but Mr. Duchemin himself, who proceeded to swear that he had not handed a copy of the Holy Gospels to Mr. Currie when the oath was administered; he simply asked him to hold up -his hand.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They are a bad crowd of lawyers in Nov-a Scotia.

Not a bad crowd of lawyers, but a bad investigator, and, in this particular case, a bad witness. This Mr. Duchemin, this splendid judicial officer whom the Government picked out to try this case with such beautiful impartiality, in order to save his good Tory friend, Mr. Currie, from the necessity of serving a term in the penitentiary, swears that he did not administer to him an oath in the manner in which it is administered in the Nova Scotia courts. The jury, however, under the direction of the judge, who instructed them that this was an oath pro forma, proceeded to find Mr. Currie, this good Tory, guilty of perjury. He was sent to the

penitentiary, and he is there now. But the Conservative organization immediately proceeded to have the case taken on a reserved question before the full Court of Nova Scotia. Here it was argued long and seriously that the evidence given by Mr. Currie was no evidence at all, because it had not been given under oath administered upon the Holy Gospels. It appeared that Mr. Duchemin at no time in any of his investigations had ever asked a witness to swear upon the Holy Gospels. What occurred? Two of the learned judges of the province of Nova Scotia, one of them in a judgment which is remarkable so far as judicial investigation upon oaths is concerned, decided that Mr. Currie had not been properly sworn by Mr. Duchemin. By a majority of one, the court decided that the oath having been an oath pro forma and having been taken by Mr. Currie with the intention of pledging himself to the truth, the charge of perjury would lie. But the Conservative organization of Nova Scotia, which had promoted the prosecutions in the counties of Guys-borough, Yarmouth-indeed, in all the counties of Nova Scotia, including that of Richmond-put up the funds necessary to, raise the issue that the methods adopted by Mr. Duchemin in swearing witnesses examined by him were wholly and totally illegal. The Conservative organization put up further funds; they carried the case to the Supreme Court of Canada, applied for a writ of habeas corpus, and asked that court to review the decision of the Nova Scotia court. The higher court held, as did the majority of the judges of the Nova Scotia court, that, an oath pro forma having been administered to this witness, and the witness having pledged himself to the truth, there was perjury in law. This gentleman, Mr. Currie, unless my hon. friends have let him out within the last day or two, as they did in the case of Landry from Richmond, is now in the penitentiary serving a term for having sworn falsely before this great inquisitor. It appeared in the course of the investigation in regard to Mr. Currie's case that Mr. Duchemin had at no time asked the witness to pledge himself to the truth by kissing the Book. So that, if my hon. friends want to be fair in regard to this matter, they ought to issue a second commission to go out and investigate Mr. Duchemin, and ascertain how many people have committed perjury in giving evidence before him.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
When you spoke of
the Conservative organization of Nova

Scotia, did you mean the provincial or the local organization?

If my hon. friend
will tell me which one it was that put up the money, I will tell him which I meant.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am a member of the executive of the provincial organization in Nova Scotia, and not one dollar was put up by that organization.

My hon. friend did
not attend all the meetings, I hope. Or is there a secret service executive of the association?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have made my statement. I know what I am talking about.

My hon. friend has
told us he knows all about it.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I do not. I simply make one statement.
Will he tell whether there is an executive committee of the provincial association of Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am a member of it.
Have you been present at all the meetings?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have not, but I know all that is going on.

My hon. friend has a system of mesmeric knowledge in regard to these things. He knows what is going on when he is not there. I presume they did not take him into their confidence when they raised this issue that the men who had purported to have sworn before Duchemin had never sworn. This particular combination of the executive knew that my hon. friend would be up here in the House and they said:	We will settle this thing without consulting John Stanfield, so he will know nothing about it. The consequence was my hon. friend Was not present when that was done. But everyone in Nova Scotia who looks at the counsel who argued the case knows that they had not done the work for nothing. They also know that Curry has no money to put up to employ counsel and also that the argument was made to save Curry from remaining in the penitentiary where he had gone. Who put up the money to make the argument before the Supreme Court? This is the kind of splendid judicial inquiries we have been having under this Government. I admire the assurance of the Minister of Marine. I would accept his word in regard to matters connected with his own province, but I want

to tell him that he should not labour under any delusion as to the status of the gentleman who conducted these inquiries in Nova Scotia. The character of these investigations is evidenced in the prosecution and detention in the penitentiary at this moment of one of the gang who went out in that province to swear away the livelihood of honest men who had been faithfully performing their duty. He had better beware of his advisers from Nova Scotia and of the character of the investigations held there under his department. The hon. member for Yarmouth called attention to a case in which my hon. friend did not find it necessary to send anyone to take an oath. I would rather see him cut off the head of anybody on the evidence of a reputable man, if he was a member of this House, than to proceed in the method in which they did in the province in connection with Mr. Duche-min's investigations. One of the first duties that every administrator of a Government has to the people who put him there is to preserve unstained the respect for the administration of justice in every form. Over and above any mere question of party political expediency or advantage to be gained for the moment through the dismissal of men to find places for party friends, stands the preservation, clear and without taint, of the administration of justice in every province. But the minister proceeded by appointing a oommis-sioner like Mr. Duchemin, who has dragged in the mire the administration of justice in Nova Scotia. The disclosures in the Curry case show that oaths were considered to be of no consequence whatever, and that statements were obtained from men under the pretence that the making of oaths in a tribunal was a mere figure of speech, which had no effect as a matter of law or of right. The Government will do better, when they want to make a dismissal, to take the word of men in this House, whose word I would accept because they are prepared to defend it; but when they go outside and take suggestions from indiscriminate quarters or appoint men to carry on the administration of justice after the manner of this tribunal, with the results I have indicated in the prosecution and detention of this man Curry and this argument before the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, they do more wrong to the whole body politic of this country in obstructing the administration of justice than they could possibly inflict in any other way.
Does the minister intend to investigate the conduct of Mr. Duchemin?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no such intention.

It is a matter of great importance, I understand, from the answer received the other day, that Mr. Duchemin is still in the employ of his department, and that if any more trials are to take place in eastern Nova Scotia, Duchemin is the man to conduct them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We hope we will have no more trials.

I have pointed out to my hon. friend that Mr. Duchemin has disregarded the law in regard to persons being represented by counsel, that he did that over and over again at the various trials in my constituency and in other constituencies in eastern Nova Scotia. 1 pointed out last year to my hon. friend that in the trial of Phillip H. Ryan, which afterwards came before the Supreme Court at Guysborough, he wilfully suppressed important evidence that he ought to have disclosed to the department at the time. My hon. friend from Pictou has pointed out his disgraceful conduct in regard to the case of Currie, who is now in the penitentiary. If the Minister of Marine will not say at this stage, after all these charges have been so specifically laid against Duchemin, that he will make an investigation into his manner of holding inquiries and also of charging fees, it will be a great disappointment to this House. The hon. member for North Cape Breton last year drew attention to a case where he tried some four people in one afternoon in some place in Cape Breton, all charged with partisanship. The whole proceeding only occupied two or three hours. He was entitled to $15 a day for his work. He split up the different trials that he held on that afternoon into four days as I understood the hon. member for North Cape Breton, and charged $60 for work for which he ought to have charged only $15. There are specific charges made against this man, over and over again, in this House and if the minister will not take any action he must be held responsible for the conduct of Duchemin.

The minister will remember that directly on coming to office he dismissed nearly all the officers in his department in the county which I represent; the fishery officers especially were



dismissed at the request of the defeated candidate, for partisanship.
When I saw my hon. friend taking that action, I took it for granted that it was based on the lofty principle of reform of the Civil Service, and that it meant that the new men appointed to the vacancies would certainly he very reticent and would attend to their duty without any interference in politics. However, knowing, as I happen to know, the men appointed, their political tendencies and their activity in elections, I hesitate to believe that their appointment will bring about reform in the Civil Service in the county of Gloucester. I may say to my hon. friend that many of these men-I can give the names if he wishes it- have been very active and even after their appointment have remained members of the organization committees in their respective homes in the county of Gloucester. They have even signed petitions for the decapitation of other officials who have been dismissed from office at their request. I put a question a few days ago to the Minister of Customs in regard to two of his officers, sub-collectors at Lameque and Tracadie, and he told me they would have to quit the political organizations. He even offered to write them immediately, advising them to retire from those organizations. I have no doubt that has been done. And would my hon. friend the Minister of Marine be not only as courteous to me, but as faithful to his principles already enunciated, to similarly notify those officials whose names I will give him if he tells me he will write them. They are men who have been very active until a few days ago. I might tell him that on the 14th of January last, just before I left home to come to this Parliament, the Conservative Association of the county of Gloucester had a meeting in Bathurst at which four or five of these officials attended.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Are they temporary or permanent officials?

They have replaced permanent officials. These men left their official positions to attend the meeting of the association for purposes of organization, and I might say that so far as my information goes, if the officials had not been there the meeting wrould have been a very small one. I do not raise any objection against the dismissals my hon. friend has made, but they must have been made upon a principle-offensive partisanship, and I *want to tell my hon. friend that ail

these officials for a long time past have	been offensive partisans	and
offensive both in nature and manners and I would like to give their names to the hon. minister:	James J. Doucet of Petit
Eocher, Edmund Arseneau of Inkerman, and Joseph O. Cbiasson of Lower Caraquet. The hon. minister should certainly appoint other men in place of these officials, and that will show that the dismissals of the past have not been made merely to punish men for being Liberals. I do not find fault with my hon. friend for appointing one of his own friends when there is a vacancy.
I myself have appointed Liberals from among my own friends. I only ask that the Government, if it really means to reform the outside civil service, should insist upon the officials sticking to their duty and if they wish to show any political activity remove them from office.

I do not want to take part in this phase of the debate to-night except to say that I am very glad indeed that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries did not find an executioner in New Brunswick like the one in Nova Scotia.
I think you will pardon me if I congratulate him along that line. I must congratulate him upon the general standing of the gentleman who occupied that position in the province of New Brunswick. While this may not be the proper time, I, want to give my friend a little information and see whether he can give me a little information. He will remember that on the St. John river, some years ago there was an arrangement made by which people were allowed to fish for salmon.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is a fisheries item..
We are dealing with the Marine items now.

I am just giving my
friend an outline so that he can look it up and let me know later. An arrangement was made I think by which they could fish for two weeks in the season. The close of the fishing season is, I think, August 14, or 15. It is a well-known fact that last year when the water was very low, the St. John had nets practically all the way across it, up in the county of Carleton, much later than the 14th of August. They were kept there right to the end of the month and even into September, and when objections were raised the reply was that they had authority to do it. I do not believe that is a fact but I wish the minister would look it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That would be impossible of course, but I will look into the matter.

I do not think myself
that they had authority but I wish to point out to the minister that he has two officials in the county of Carleton who are simply a disgrace.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Who are they?

One man's name is
Parker. I have not seen them fishing myself, but I am told by responsible people that they fished in season and out of season.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Will you give me the name of the other man?
Mr-. CARVELL:	I will get it for you.
These men I am told-and I would not make a statement like this publicly if I did not have some grounds for saying so- fish in season and out of season. They are well known poachers and succeeded in getting appointed for the simple purpose of poaching and allowing their friends and relatives to poach; and I wish my hon. friend would see if any such instructions or authority were given. While I do not believe they were, I want to be sure when this matter comes before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will certainly get the
information for my hon. friend as the charge which he has made is, of course, a very serious one against men appointed to protect the fisheries. No time will be lost by my department in investigating the matter and finding out if there is any truth in it; and if such is the case, those men will not be allowed to continue in the department for a single minute.
I have lots of evidence.

What is the attitude of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to be towards persons appointed to office by him and who are found to be notorious partisans. Will he insist that these persons shall refrain from taking part in political work during their incumbency of office?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no doubt my hon. friend, when he gets into office, will turn them out very speedily.

I am glad to know that the minister understands my character so well. That is what I would insist upon doing. If a man wants to interfere in politics he must take the responsibility of giving up his official position. That is the stand I have always taken, and, should I continue to be in public life and should my party come back to power, I shall adhere to that stand. But I would like to set- an answer 50i
from the minister on that subject. We had an answer from the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) last year. He was frank enough to say that he would not permit any partisanship on the part of any official appointed to office by him. I would like to know if the minister agrees with the position taken by the Postmaster General.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I certainly agree with him.

Then, I would inform the minister that an official of his department, appointed by him, in St. Peter's, was recently elected secretary of the Conservative Association for the county of Richmond. I would like the minister to take note of that matter and to give this official the choice between his official and political offices.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Certainly, if the hon. gentleman will give me the name. -

Dr. John A. Macdonald,
.junior, port physician of the harbour of St. Peter's, who was, in the month of December last, elected to the position of secretary of the Conservative Association for that county.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
Monday, Feburary 16, 1914.
